</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

Notice that we are given that

$$
{x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{t}.
$$

We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-2t} & 2{e}^{t} \\ 2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix},\,f(t)=\begin{bmatrix}12t \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{-2t}\cdot {e}^{t}-2{e}^{t}\cdot 2{e}^{-2t}}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} & -2{e}^{t} \\ -2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{t}}{3}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} & -2{e}^{t} \\ -2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & -2{e}^{2t} \\ -2{e}^{-t} & {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix} \\ {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =-\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & -2{e}^{2t} \\ -2{e}^{-t} & {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}12t \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-4t{e}^{2t} \\ 8t{e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \begin{bmatrix}-4t{e}^{2t} \\ 8t{e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\int -4t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int 8t{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating the components by parts, we get the following:

- For the first component, let $u=-4t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=-4\,\text{d}t$ and $v=\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -4t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t & =(-4t)\cdot \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}-\int \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}\cdot (-4\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-2t{e}^{2t}+\int 2{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-2t{e}^{2t}+{e}^{2t} \\  & ={e}^{2t}(1-2t).\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, let $u=8t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=8\,\text{d}t$ and $v=-{e}^{-t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -4t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t & =8t\cdot (-{e}^{-t})-\int -{e}^{-t}\cdot 8\,\text{d}t \\  & =-8t{e}^{-t}+\int 8\,{e}^{-t}\text{d}t \\  & =-8t{e}^{-t}-8{e}^{2t} \\  & =-8{e}^{-t}(1+t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-2t} & 2{e}^{t} \\ 2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t}(1-2t) \\ -8{e}^{-t}(1+t)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}(1-2t)-16(1+t) \\ 2(1-2t)-8(1+t)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-18t-15 \\ -12t-6\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "7c983da7-ca72-5a73-bf3a-e7f56ec9519d" :step/next {:db/id 17592186497428}} {:db/id 17592186497452 :step/content {:db/id 17592186365792 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "ff2cccf5-489b-5e70-b3a9-9d2661562299" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2{e}^{-3t}" :db/id 17592186365794} {:answer/id #uuid "4c7d0200-75d6-56dc-9a3b-832b6fae8337" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2e^{-3t}" :db/id 17592186496829}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186496829} :answer-field/id #uuid "ef783e3c-2210-5313-90c8-cc217b3c7be3" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186365793} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "974ddd49-be50-5576-a845-339cab6a2a08" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4/3" :db/id 17592186365796} {:answer/id #uuid "0aacdf65-443f-56da-b835-155b66a57197" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4}{3}" :db/id 17592186496676}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186496676} :answer-field/id #uuid "c4dc56ff-d11b-5257-828e-dfd7f038bf79" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186365795}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "cab04d20-21da-5031-a5e8-e08eadd456c5" :question/math-academy-id "q-336698" :question/problem "$$

$$

$$

We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{t} \\ 3{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix},\,f(t)=\begin{bmatrix}5t \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{2{e}^{-2t}\cdot {e}^{t}-{e}^{t}\cdot 3{e}^{-2t}}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} & -{e}^{t} \\ -3{e}^{-2t} & 2{e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =-{e}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} & -{e}^{t} \\ -3{e}^{-2t} & 2{e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =-\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & -{e}^{2t} \\ -3{e}^{-t} & 2{e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =-\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & -{e}^{2t} \\ -3{e}^{-t} & 2{e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5t \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-5t{e}^{2t} \\ 15t{e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \begin{bmatrix}-5t{e}^{2t} \\ 15t{e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\int -5t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int 15t{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating the components by parts, we get the following:

- For the first component, let $u=-5t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=-5\,\text{d}t$ and $v=\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -5t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t & =(-5t)\cdot \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}-\int \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}\cdot (-5\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-\frac{5}{2}t{e}^{2t}+\frac{5}{2}\int {e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{5}{2}t{e}^{2t}+\frac{5}{4}{e}^{2t} \\  & =\frac{5}{4}{e}^{2t}(1-2t).\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, let $u=15t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=15\,\text{d}t$ and $v=-{e}^{-t}.$ So,

$$

$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)

$$

$$

We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}],\,f(t)=[\begin{aligned}3t \\ t\end{aligned}].
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{-3t}\cdot {e}^{-t}-0}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={e}^{4t}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{t}\end{aligned}]. \\ {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3t \\ t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3t{e}^{3t} \\ t{e}^{t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int [\begin{aligned}3t{e}^{3t} \\ t{e}^{t}\end{aligned}]\,\text{d}t \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\int 3t{e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating the components by parts, we get the following:

- For the first component, let $u=3t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=3\,\text{d}t$ and $v=\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 3t{e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t & =(3t)\cdot \frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}-\int \frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}(3\,\text{d}t) \\  & =t{e}^{3t}-\int {e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =t{e}^{3t}-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}(3t-1).\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, let $u=t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=1\,\text{d}t$ and $v={e}^{t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t & =t\cdot {e}^{t}-\int {e}^{t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =t{e}^{t}-{e}^{t} \\  & ={e}^{t}(t-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

:question/math-academy-id "q-336713" :question/problem "Consider the following system of differential equations:

$$

$$

Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t),$ where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and $u(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for ${x}_{p}(t)$ is given below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from the fact that {{field-1}} matrix.

$\,$ Line $\text{L5}$ follows from lines {{field-2}} by substitution.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ by {{field-3}} both sides of the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting {{field-4}} into $\text{L1}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider line $\text{L4}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are solutions to the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ i.e., by substituting any column $c(t)$ of $Φ$ into the homogeneous system, we get

$$
{c}^{′}(t)=Ac(t),
$$

where ${c}^{′}(t)$ is the corresponding column of derivatives in $Φ.$ As a result, this means that ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ.$ Therefore, $\text{L4}$ follows from the fact that $Φ\text{ is a fundamental}$ matrix.

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L3}$, $\text{L4},$ and $\text{L5}.$ Let's substitute ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$ from $\text{L4}$ into $\text{L3}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)+\cancel{AΦu(t)}=\cancel{AΦu(t)}+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L3}\text{ and }\text{L4}$ by substitution.

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ To get $\text{L7},$ we are $\text{integrating}$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L6}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int {Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)\,\text{d}t \\ u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L7},$ and $\text{L8}.$ Substituting

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

from $\text{L7}$ into $\text{L1},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φu(t) \\  & =Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L7}$ into $\text{L1}.$"} :step/id #uuid "1464fa05-0d62-5c01-b491-e56ce5c8e2e8" :step/next {:db/id 17592186515692}} {:db/id 17592186515651 :step/content {:db/id 17592186311832 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c5b84d3b-c2a0-5c17-a951-7b667223d9c2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4t-5" :db/id 17592186310336}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186310336} :answer-field/id #uuid "f75ca1ce-9660-5f2b-8e80-e3b967d7673c" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186311515}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "1a119389-1e86-5899-9ba6-43b2c31d6800" :question/math-academy-id "q-337288" :question/problem "$$

|  | $6t-6$ |  |  |  |" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

Notice that we are given that

$$
{x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-t}.
$$

We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{-t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix},\,f(t)=\begin{bmatrix}t \\ 3t\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{-2t}\cdot {e}^{-t}-{e}^{-t}\cdot 0}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-t} & -{e}^{-t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={e}^{3t}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-t} & -{e}^{-t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & -{e}^{2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & -{e}^{2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}t \\ 3t\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2t{e}^{2t} \\ 3t{e}^{t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \begin{bmatrix}-2t{e}^{2t} \\ 3t{e}^{t}\end{bmatrix}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\int -2t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int 3t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating the components by parts, we get the following:

- For the first component, let $u=-2t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=-2\,\text{d}t$ and $v=\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -2t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t & =(-2t)\cdot \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}-\int \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}\cdot (-2\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-t{e}^{2t}+\int {e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-t{e}^{2t}+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}(1-2t).\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, let $u=3t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=3\,\text{d}t$ and $v={e}^{t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 3t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t & =(3t)\cdot {e}^{t}-\int {e}^{t}\cdot (3\,\text{d}t) \\  & =3t{e}^{t}-3{e}^{t} \\  & =3{e}^{t}(t-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{-t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}(1-2t) \\ 3{e}^{t}(t-1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}(1-2t)+6(t-1) \\ 6(t-1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}4t-5 \\ 6t-6\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "4f772438-7511-5d11-8498-5f7b2fa9adee"} {:db/id 17592186515692 :step/content {:db/id 17592186311828 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "38e50ee6-2518-5d34-a3e2-4799e3d17703" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5{e}^{2t}" :db/id 17592186309180}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186309180} :answer-field/id #uuid "573e1e64-9846-5e0e-bb82-38a0518ddaaf" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186311021} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "7781a288-b83b-5516-8d03-ce94842577fc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{-1}{3}" :db/id 17592186309684}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186309684} :answer-field/id #uuid "7a42318d-7765-5b03-b495-8b35312f578c" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186311126}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "6ac8d1ba-163b-54eb-addd-dba5b1956964" :question/math-academy-id "q-337280" :question/problem "$$

$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

Notice that we are given that

$$
{x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}.
$$

We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}],\,f(t)=[\begin{aligned}3t \\ t\end{aligned}].
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{-3t}\cdot {e}^{-t}-0}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={e}^{4t}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{t}\end{aligned}]. \\ {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3t \\ t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3t{e}^{3t} \\ t{e}^{t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int [\begin{aligned}3t{e}^{3t} \\ t{e}^{t}\end{aligned}]\,\text{d}t \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\int 3t{e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating the components by parts, we get the following:

- For the first component, let $u=3t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=3\,\text{d}t$ and $v=\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 3t{e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t & =(3t)\cdot \frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}-\int \frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}(3\,\text{d}t) \\  & =t{e}^{3t}-\int {e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =t{e}^{3t}-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}(3t-1).\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, let $u=t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=1\,\text{d}t$ and $v={e}^{t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t & =t\cdot {e}^{t}-\int {e}^{t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =t{e}^{t}-{e}^{t} \\  & ={e}^{t}(t-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}(3t-1) \\ {e}^{t}(t-1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}3t-1 \\ 3(t-1)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

$\,$ Line $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting {{field-4}} into $\text{L1}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's examine each statement in turn.

"q-337280" :question/problem "$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 \\ -5 & -1\end{bmatrix}x(t)+\overset{f(t)}{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} \\ 4{e}^{t}\end{bmatrix}}},\,Φ=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 3{e}^{4t} \\ {e}^{-t} & -3{e}^{4t}\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the system of differential equations and the fundamental matrix of the corresponding homogeneous system above. Using the method of variation of parameters, compute ${Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)$ and the particular solution ${x}_{p}(t)$ of the system.

| ${Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)=\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} |  | $\,,\,$ | ${x}_{p}(t)={e}^{t}\,\,$ |  | {{field-2}} |  |  |

$$

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 3{e}^{4t} \\ {e}^{-t} & -3{e}^{4t}\end{bmatrix},\,f(t)=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} \\ 4{e}^{t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{0\cdot (-3{e}^{4t})-3{e}^{4t}\cdot {e}^{-t}}\begin{bmatrix}-3{e}^{4t} & -3{e}^{4t} \\ -{e}^{-t} & 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-3t}}{3}\begin{bmatrix}-3{e}^{4t} & -3{e}^{4t} \\ -{e}^{-t} & 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} & {e}^{t} \\ \frac{1}{3}{e}^{-4t} & 0\end{bmatrix} \\ {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} & {e}^{t} \\ \frac{1}{3}{e}^{-4t} & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} \\ 4{e}^{t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5{e}^{2t} \\ \frac{1}{3}{e}^{-3t}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \begin{bmatrix}5{e}^{2t} \\ \frac{1}{3}{e}^{-3t}\end{bmatrix}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\int 5{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int \frac{1}{3}{e}^{-3t}\,\text{d}t\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{5}{2}{e}^{2t} \\ -\frac{1}{9}{e}^{-3t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 3{e}^{4t} \\ {e}^{-t} & -3{e}^{4t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{5}{2}{e}^{2t} \\ -\frac{1}{9}{e}^{-3t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{t} \\ \frac{17}{6}{e}^{t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={e}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{17}{6}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "c1f84e26-b520-572d-b1af-861828868756" :step/next {:db/id 17592186515622}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c5b84d3b-c2a0-5c17-a951-7b667223d9c2" :answer/type {:db/id "q-337219" :question/problem "$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}3 & -2 \\ 2 & -2\end{bmatrix}x(t)+\begin{bmatrix}5t \\ 7t\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the system of differential equations. Using the method of variation of parameters, the general solution of the equation can be written in the form

| $x(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{2t}+\,\,\frac{1}{4}$ |  | $8t-14$ |  | . |

|  | {{field-1}} |  |  |  |" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

Notice that we are given that

$$
{x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{2t}.
$$

We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-t} & 2{e}^{2t} \\ 2{e}^{-t} & {e}^{2t}\end{bmatrix},\,f(t)=\begin{bmatrix}5t \\ 7t\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{-t}\cdot {e}^{2t}-2{e}^{2t}\cdot 2{e}^{-t}}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & -2{e}^{2t} \\ -2{e}^{-t} & {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-t}}{3}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & -2{e}^{2t} \\ -2{e}^{-t} & {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}-{e}^{t} & 2{e}^{t} \\ 2{e}^{-2t} & -{e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix} \\ {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}-{e}^{t} & 2{e}^{t} \\ 2{e}^{-2t} & -{e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5t \\ 7t\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3t{e}^{t} \\ t{e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \begin{bmatrix}3t{e}^{t} \\ t{e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\int 3t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int t{e}^{-2t}\,\text{d}t\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating the components by parts, we get the following:

- For the first component, let $u=3t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=3\,\text{d}t$ and $v={e}^{t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 3t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t & =(3t)\cdot {e}^{t}-\int {e}^{t}\cdot (3\,\text{d}t) \\  & =3t{e}^{t}-3{e}^{t} \\  & =3{e}^{t}(t-1).\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, let $u=t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{-2t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=1\,\text{d}t$ and $v=-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-2t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int t{e}^{-2t}\,\text{d}t & =(t)\cdot (-\frac{{e}^{-2t}}{2})-\int (-\frac{{e}^{-2t}}{2})\cdot (1\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-\frac{t{e}^{-2t}}{2}-\frac{{e}^{-2t}}{4} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-2t}}{4}(2t+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-t} & 2{e}^{2t} \\ 2{e}^{-t} & {e}^{2t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3{e}^{t}(t-1) \\ -\frac{{e}^{-2t}}{4}(2t+1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix}12(t-1)-2(2t+1) \\ 24(t-1)-(2t+1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix}8t-14 \\ 22t-25\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "25f637fb-d499-5964-98b0-d92aa3739826" :step/next {:db/id 17592186531681}} {:db/id 17592186531679 :step/content {:db/id 17592186531596 :question/answer-fields "q-336703" :question/problem "Consider the following system of differential equations:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)
$$

Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t),$ where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and $u(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for ${x}_{p}(t)$ is given below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}$ into the {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from line $\text{L5}$ by {{field-2}} both sides of the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ by {{field-3}} both sides of the equation." :question/worked-solution "Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L2},$ and $\text{L3}.$ Let's substitute ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$ from $\text{L1}$ and ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$ from $\text{L2}$ into the initial system of ODEs:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =Ax(t)+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t) & =AΦu(t)+f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}$ into $\text{initial system of ODEs}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L5}$ and $\text{L6}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are linearly independent. So, $Φ$ is invertible. Therefore, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by $\text{pre-multiplying by }{Φ}^{-1}$ both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\cdot Φ{u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ ({Φ}^{-1}Φ)\cdot {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ To get $\text{L7},$ we are $\text{integrating}$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L6}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int {Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)\,\text{d}t \\ u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "2cb68189-e6bd-50df-bf7a-85be4d333c8d" :step/next {:db/id 17592186531674}} {:db/id 17592186531681 :step/content {:db/id 17592186311821 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "98d66787-66e5-569a-91da-fb16e858ec7d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-8{e}^{-4t}" :db/id 17592186309980}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186309980} :answer-field/id #uuid "33380138-39c7-5cc1-be02-40c0352385d9" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186310928} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "57fa1d40-985b-5dc8-bff3-11325100380c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186309411}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186309411} :answer-field/id #uuid "74228cec-035c-567c-bcee-7a90efcf66d3" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186311105}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "3c98926c-5044-5e94-be2a-fc638fdc3f93" :question/math-academy-id "q-337230" :question/problem "$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{4t}\end{bmatrix},\,f(t)=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -8\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{t}\cdot {e}^{4t}-0\cdot 0}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{4t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={e}^{-5t}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{4t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{-4t}\end{bmatrix}. \\ {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{-4t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -8\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{-t} \\ -8{e}^{-4t}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{-t} \\ -8{e}^{-4t}\end{bmatrix}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\int 2{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int -8{e}^{-4t}\,\text{d}t\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2{e}^{-t} \\ 2{e}^{-4t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$

|  | {{field-1}} |  |  |  |" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

Notice that we are given that

$$
{x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{t}.
$$

We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-2t} & -{e}^{t} \\ 2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix},\,f(t)=\begin{bmatrix}4t \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{-2t}\cdot {e}^{t}-(-{e}^{t})\cdot 2{e}^{-2t}}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} & {e}^{t} \\ -2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{t}}{3}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} & {e}^{t} \\ -2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & {e}^{2t} \\ -2{e}^{-t} & {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & {e}^{2t} \\ -2{e}^{-t} & {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4t \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{4}{3}t{e}^{2t} \\ -\frac{8}{3}t{e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \begin{bmatrix}\frac{4}{3}t{e}^{2t} \\ -\frac{8}{3}t{e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\int \frac{4}{3}t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int -\frac{8}{3}t{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating the components by parts, we get the following:

- For the first component, let $u=\frac{4}{3}t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=\frac{4}{3}\,\text{d}t$ and $v=\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{4}{3}t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t & =\frac{4}{3}t\cdot \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}-\int \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}\cdot (\frac{4}{3}\,\text{d}t) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}t{e}^{2t}-\frac{2}{3}\int {e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{2}{3}t{e}^{2t}-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{2t} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{e}^{2t}(2t-1).\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, let $u=-\frac{8}{3}t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=-\frac{8}{3}\,\text{d}t$ and $v=-{e}^{-t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -\frac{8}{3}t{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t & =-\frac{8}{3}t\cdot (-{e}^{-t})-\int -{e}^{-t}\cdot (-\frac{8}{3}\,\text{d}t) \\  & =\frac{8}{3}t{e}^{-t}-\frac{8}{3}\int {e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{8}{3}t{e}^{-t}+\frac{8}{3}{e}^{-t} \\  & =\frac{8}{3}{e}^{-t}(t+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-2t} & -{e}^{t} \\ 2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{3}{e}^{2t}(2t-1) \\ \frac{8}{3}{e}^{-t}(t+1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}(2t-1)-8(t+1) \\ 2(2t-1)+8(t+1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2t-3 \\ 4t+2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "c5d20bf1-c67d-533b-b7e7-2dfd3e6fc008"} {:db/id 17592186531717 :step/content {:db/id 17592186531573 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8535759b-fe73-52af-853f-f3486f41d48a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2e^{-2t}" :db/id 17592186531153}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186531153} :answer-field/id #uuid "57ab610c-28ab-5d09-83f7-d68b274b353d" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186531452} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "f89927db-d31d-51e0-b063-5d1318a6634f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186531369}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186531369} :answer-field/id #uuid "9aa355cf-d45f-5b54-bcec-6c9a1e489b0d" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186531489}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "29e3e5d7-28ea-5e8a-b874-caa92a5ebba1" :question/math-academy-id "q-336597" :question/problem "$$

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

Notice that we are given that

$$
{x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{2t}.
$$

We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-t} & 2{e}^{2t} \\ 2{e}^{-t} & {e}^{2t}\end{bmatrix},\,f(t)=\begin{bmatrix}5t \\ 7t\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{-t}\cdot {e}^{2t}-2{e}^{2t}\cdot 2{e}^{-t}}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & -2{e}^{2t} \\ -2{e}^{-t} & {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-t}}{3}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & -2{e}^{2t} \\ -2{e}^{-t} & {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}-{e}^{t} & 2{e}^{t} \\ 2{e}^{-2t} & -{e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix} \\ {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}-{e}^{t} & 2{e}^{t} \\ 2{e}^{-2t} & -{e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5t \\ 7t\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3t{e}^{t} \\ t{e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \begin{bmatrix}3t{e}^{t} \\ t{e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\int 3t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int t{e}^{-2t}\,\text{d}t\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating the components by parts, we get the following:

- For the first component, let $u=3t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=3\,\text{d}t$ and $v={e}^{t}.$ So,

$$

$$

$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-t} & 2{e}^{2t} \\ 2{e}^{-t} & {e}^{2t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3{e}^{t}(t-1) \\ -\frac{{e}^{-2t}}{4}(2t+1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix}12(t-1)-2(2t+1) \\ 24(t-1)-(2t+1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix}8t-14 \\ 22t-25\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

"q-336703" :question/problem "Consider the following system of differential equations:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)
$$

Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t),$ where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and $u(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for ${x}_{p}(t)$ is given below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}$ into the {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from line $\text{L5}$ by {{field-2}} both sides of the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ by {{field-3}} both sides of the equation." :question/worked-solution "Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L2},$ and $\text{L3}.$ Let's substitute ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$ from $\text{L1}$ and ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$ from $\text{L2}$ into the initial system of ODEs:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =Ax(t)+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t) & =AΦu(t)+f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}$ into $\text{initial system of ODEs}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L5}$ and $\text{L6}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are linearly independent. So, $Φ$ is invertible. Therefore, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by $\text{pre-multiplying by }{Φ}^{-1}$ both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\cdot Φ{u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ ({Φ}^{-1}Φ)\cdot {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ To get $\text{L7},$ we are $\text{integrating}$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L6}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int {Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)\,\text{d}t \\ u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "2cb68189-e6bd-50df-bf7a-85be4d333c8d" :step/next {:db/id 17592186531674}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "91ab3da8-8b65-5c7c-b413-f64ac221623d" :answer/type {:db/id |  | {{field-1}} |  |  |  |" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

Notice that we are given that

$$
{x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{t}.
$$

We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-2t} & -{e}^{t} \\ 2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix},\,f(t)=\begin{bmatrix}4t \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{-2t}\cdot {e}^{t}-(-{e}^{t})\cdot 2{e}^{-2t}}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} & {e}^{t} \\ -2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{t}}{3}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} & {e}^{t} \\ -2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & {e}^{2t} \\ -2{e}^{-t} & {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & {e}^{2t} \\ -2{e}^{-t} & {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4t \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{4}{3}t{e}^{2t} \\ -\frac{8}{3}t{e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \begin{bmatrix}\frac{4}{3}t{e}^{2t} \\ -\frac{8}{3}t{e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\int \frac{4}{3}t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int -\frac{8}{3}t{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating the components by parts, we get the following:

- For the first component, let $u=\frac{4}{3}t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=\frac{4}{3}\,\text{d}t$ and $v=\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{4}{3}t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t & =\frac{4}{3}t\cdot \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}-\int \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}\cdot (\frac{4}{3}\,\text{d}t) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}t{e}^{2t}-\frac{2}{3}\int {e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{2}{3}t{e}^{2t}-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{2t} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{e}^{2t}(2t-1).\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, let $u=-\frac{8}{3}t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=-\frac{8}{3}\,\text{d}t$ and $v=-{e}^{-t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -\frac{8}{3}t{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t & =-\frac{8}{3}t\cdot (-{e}^{-t})-\int -{e}^{-t}\cdot (-\frac{8}{3}\,\text{d}t) \\  & =\frac{8}{3}t{e}^{-t}-\frac{8}{3}\int {e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{8}{3}t{e}^{-t}+\frac{8}{3}{e}^{-t} \\  & =\frac{8}{3}{e}^{-t}(t+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-2t} & -{e}^{t} \\ 2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{3}{e}^{2t}(2t-1) \\ \frac{8}{3}{e}^{-t}(t+1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}(2t-1)-8(t+1) \\ 2(2t-1)+8(t+1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2t-3 \\ 4t+2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "c5d20bf1-c67d-533b-b7e7-2dfd3e6fc008"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "ca5fb1c3-f4d9-5a37-a9bd-6708fe402752" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4t+2" :question/math-academy-id "q-336712" :question/problem "Consider the following system of differential equations:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)
$$

Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t),$ where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and $u(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for ${x}_{p}(t)$ is given below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from the fact that {{field-1}} matrix.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ by {{field-2}} both sides of the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting {{field-3}} into {{field-4}}." :question/worked-solution "Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first we consider line $\text{L4}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are solutions to the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ i.e., by substituting any column $c(t)$ of $Φ$ into the homogeneous system, we get

$$
{c}^{′}(t)=Ac(t),
$$

where ${c}^{′}(t)$ is the corresponding column of derivatives in $Φ.$ As a result, this means that ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ.$ Therefore, $\text{L4}$ follows from the fact that $Φ\text{ is a fundamental}$ matrix.

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ To get $\text{L7},$ we are $\text{integrating}$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L6}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int {Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)\,\text{d}t \\ u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L7},$ and $\text{L8}.$ Substituting

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

from $\text{L7}$ into $\text{L1},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φu(t) \\  & =Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L7}$ into $\text{L1}.$"} :step/id #uuid "060efb46-b822-5dba-9e37-6c83cd83dada" :step/next {:db/id 17592186543604}} {:db/id 17592186543604 :step/content {:db/id 17592186311831 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "d356bc26-57d5-59ea-80f6-ad3d535a1609" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "36t-24" :db/id 17592186310448}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186310448} :answer-field/id #uuid "b2e3e1f1-67f2-5abf-8891-7159f370a35a" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186311312}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "6ed0b294-0a14-518d-b751-a90930d00a2e" :question/math-academy-id "q-337287" :question/problem "$$

$$
{x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}{e}^{3t}.
$$

We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-t} & {e}^{3t} \\ {e}^{-t} & 3{e}^{3t}\end{bmatrix},\,f(t)=\begin{bmatrix}2t \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{-t}\cdot 3{e}^{3t}-{e}^{3t}\cdot {e}^{-t}}\begin{bmatrix}3{e}^{3t} & -{e}^{3t} \\ -{e}^{-t} & {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2{e}^{2t}}\begin{bmatrix}3{e}^{3t} & -{e}^{3t} \\ -{e}^{-t} & {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}3{e}^{t} & -{e}^{t} \\ -{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-3t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}3{e}^{t} & -{e}^{t} \\ -{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-3t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2t \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3t{e}^{t} \\ -t{e}^{-3t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \begin{bmatrix}3t{e}^{t} \\ -t{e}^{-3t}\end{bmatrix}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\int 3t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int -t{e}^{-3t}\,\text{d}t\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

- For the first component, let $u=3t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=3\,\text{d}t$ and $v={e}^{t}.$ So,

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$\text{L1}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L3}$, $\text{L4},$ and $\text{L5}.$ Let's substitute ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$ from $\text{L4}$ into $\text{L3}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)+\cancel{AΦu(t)}=\cancel{AΦu(t)}+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L3}\text{ and }\text{L4}$ by substitution.

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L7},$ and $\text{L8}.$ Substituting

"Consider the following system of differential equations:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)
$$

Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t),$ where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and $u(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for ${x}_{p}(t)$ is given below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by {{field-1}} both sides of  the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}$ into the {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from the fact that {{field-3}} matrix." :question/worked-solution "Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ To get $\text{L2},$ we are $\text{differentiating}$ with respect to $t$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}^{′}(t) & =(Φu(t))^{′} \\ {x}_{p}^{′}(t) & =Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L2},$ and $\text{L3}.$ Let's substitute ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$ from $\text{L1}$ and ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$ from $\text{L2}$ into the initial system of ODEs:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =Ax(t)+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t) & =AΦu(t)+f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}$ into $\text{initial system of ODEs}.$

- Finally we consider line $\text{L4}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are solutions to the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ i.e., by substituting any column $c(t)$ of $Φ$ into the homogeneous system, we get

$$
{c}^{′}(t)=Ac(t),
$$

where ${c}^{′}(t)$ is the corresponding column of derivatives in $Φ.$ As a result, this means that ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ.$ Therefore, $\text{L4}$ follows from the fact that $Φ\text{ is a fundamental}$ matrix."} |  | {{field-1}} |  |  |  |" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

Notice that we are given that

$$
{x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}{e}^{3t}.
$$

We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-t} & {e}^{3t} \\ {e}^{-t} & 3{e}^{3t}\end{bmatrix},\,f(t)=\begin{bmatrix}2t \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{-t}\cdot 3{e}^{3t}-{e}^{3t}\cdot {e}^{-t}}\begin{bmatrix}3{e}^{3t} & -{e}^{3t} \\ -{e}^{-t} & {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2{e}^{2t}}\begin{bmatrix}3{e}^{3t} & -{e}^{3t} \\ -{e}^{-t} & {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}3{e}^{t} & -{e}^{t} \\ -{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-3t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}3{e}^{t} & -{e}^{t} \\ -{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-3t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2t \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3t{e}^{t} \\ -t{e}^{-3t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \begin{bmatrix}3t{e}^{t} \\ -t{e}^{-3t}\end{bmatrix}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\int 3t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int -t{e}^{-3t}\,\text{d}t\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating the components by parts, we get the following:

- For the first component, let $u=3t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=3\,\text{d}t$ and $v={e}^{t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 3t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t & =(3t)\cdot {e}^{t}-\int {e}^{t}\cdot (3\,\text{d}t) \\  & =3t{e}^{t}-3{e}^{t} \\  & =3{e}^{t}(t-1).\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, let $u=-t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{-3t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=-\,\text{d}t$ and $v=-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-3t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -t{e}^{-3t}\,\text{d}t & =(-t)\cdot (-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-3t})-\int (-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-3t})\cdot (-\,\text{d}t) \\  & =\frac{t}{3}{e}^{-3t}-\frac{1}{3}\int {e}^{-3t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{t}{3}{e}^{-3t}+\frac{1}{9}{e}^{-3t} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}{e}^{-3t}(3t+1).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-t} & {e}^{3t} \\ {e}^{-t} & 3{e}^{3t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3{e}^{t}(t-1) \\ \frac{1}{9}{e}^{-3t}(3t+1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\begin{bmatrix}27(t-1)+(3t+1) \\ 27(t-1)+3(3t+1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\begin{bmatrix}30t-26 \\ 36t-24\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

where ${c}^{′}(t)$ is the corresponding column of derivatives in $Φ.$ As a result, this means that ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ.$ Therefore, $\text{L4}$ follows from the fact that $Φ\text{ is a fundamental}$ matrix."} "4ee21254-0061-505a-86c2-50174dc611d2" :question/math-academy-id "q-336715" :question/problem "Consider the following system of differential equations:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)
$$

Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t),$ where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and $u(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for ${x}_{p}(t)$ is given below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}$ into the {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from line $\text{L5}$ by {{field-2}} both sides of the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ by {{field-3}} both sides of the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L7}$ into {{field-4}} ." :question/worked-solution "Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L2},$ and $\text{L3}.$ Let's substitute ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$ from $\text{L1}$ and ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$ from $\text{L2}$ into the initial system of ODEs:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =Ax(t)+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t) & =AΦu(t)+f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}$ into $\text{initial system of ODEs}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L5}$ and $\text{L6}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are linearly independent. So, $Φ$ is invertible. Therefore, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by $\text{pre-multiplying by }{Φ}^{-1}$ both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\cdot Φ{u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ ({Φ}^{-1}Φ)\cdot {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ To get $\text{L7},$ we are $\text{integrating}$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L6}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int {Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)\,\text{d}t \\ u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L7},$ and $\text{L8}.$ Substituting

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

from $\text{L7}$ into $\text{L1},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φu(t) \\  & =Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L7}$ into  $\text{L1}.$"} :step/id #uuid "05075f15-5b66-59aa-85c7-2761de8fc384" :step/next {:db/id 17592186552532}} {:db/id 17592186552532 "q-336716" :question/problem "Consider the following system of differential equations:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)
$$

Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t),$ where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and $u(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for ${x}_{p}(t)$ is given below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by {{field-1}} both sides of  the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ by {{field-2}} both sides of the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting {{field-3}} into {{field-4}}." :question/worked-solution "Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ To get $\text{L2},$ we are $\text{differentiating}$ with respect to $t$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}^{′}(t) & =(Φu(t))^{′} \\ {x}_{p}^{′}(t) & =Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ To get $\text{L7},$ we are $\text{integrating}$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L6}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int {Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)\,\text{d}t \\ u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L7},$ and $\text{L8}.$ Substituting

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

from $\text{L7}$ into $\text{L1},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φu(t) \\  & =Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L7}$ into $\text{L1}.$"} :step/id #uuid "092c6a00-72eb-562b-a6ec-edba31e0a817"} {:db/id 17592186552554 :step/content {:db/id 17592186167184 Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t),$ where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and $u(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for ${x}_{p}(t)$ is given below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from the fact that {{field-1}} matrix.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from line $\text{L5}$ by {{field-2}} both sides of the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ by {{field-3}} both sides of the equation." :question/worked-solution "Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider line $\text{L4}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are solutions to the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ i.e., by substituting any column $c(t)$ of $Φ$ into the homogeneous system, we get

$$
{c}^{′}(t)=Ac(t),
$$

where ${c}^{′}(t)$ is the corresponding column of derivatives in $Φ.$ As a result, this means that ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ.$ Therefore, $\text{L4}$ follows from the fact that $Φ\text{ is a fundamental}$ matrix.

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L5}$ and $\text{L6}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are linearly independent. So, $Φ$ is invertible. Therefore, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by $\text{multiplying by }{Φ}^{-1}$ both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\cdot Φ{u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ ({Φ}^{-1}Φ)\cdot {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ To get $\text{L7},$ we are $\text{integrating}$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L6}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int {Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)\,\text{d}t \\ u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "3e6e22b3-4760-5866-a573-0523c5c9013b" :step/next {:db/id 17592186552559}} {:db/id 17592186552559 :step/content {:db/id 17592186167185 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "eabf843f-76af-5374-87f3-015cd7c21177" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186365600}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186365600} :answer-field/id #uuid "2b0824a7-3977-53c2-8ae9-fab24fac62a7" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186365599} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0e7d357d-8554-535e-9625-2f454e5a740e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-4{e}^{-4t}" :db/id 17592186365602} {:answer/id #uuid "2014d6d7-4139-5c85-9128-fa0bef9f20e7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-4e^{-4t}" :db/id 17592186482873}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186482873} :answer-field/id #uuid "e2490d5f-d96a-5160-b6f7-a7d11c4a92d8" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186365601}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "a01f2ab9-e122-54f4-be8c-8d60cf41b11c" :question/math-academy-id "q-330893" :question/problem "$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}2 & -3 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}x(t)+\overset{f(t)}{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -8\end{bmatrix}}},\,Φ=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & -3{e}^{4t} \\ 0 & 2{e}^{4t}\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the system of differential equations and the fundamental matrix of the corresponding homogeneous system above. Using the method of variation of parameters, compute ${Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)$ and the particular solution ${x}_{p}(t)$ of the system.

<td align="center">$-10{e}^{-2t}$</td>
<td align="center" width="5px"></td>

<td align="center" height="40px" rowspan="2">${x}_{p}(t)=\,\,$</td>

<td align="center"></td>

</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & -3{e}^{4t} \\ 0 & 2{e}^{4t}\end{bmatrix},\,f(t)=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -8\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{2t}\cdot 2{e}^{4t}-(-3{e}^{4t})\cdot 0}\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{4t} & 3{e}^{4t} \\ 0 & {e}^{2t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-6t}}{2}\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{4t} & 3{e}^{4t} \\ 0 & {e}^{2t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{-2t} & 3{e}^{-2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-4t}\end{bmatrix} \\ {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{-2t} & 3{e}^{-2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-4t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -8\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-10{e}^{-2t} \\ -4{e}^{-4t}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \begin{bmatrix}-10{e}^{-2t} \\ -4{e}^{-4t}\end{bmatrix}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\int -10{e}^{-2t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int -4{e}^{-4t}\,\text{d}t\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5{e}^{-2t} \\ {e}^{-4t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & -3{e}^{4t} \\ 0 & 2{e}^{4t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5{e}^{-2t} \\ {e}^{-4t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "5095702a-0e43-5e39-ba55-42ec3c14effd" :step/next {:db/id 17592186552603}} {:db/id 17592186552603 :step/content {:db/id 17592186552459 :question/answer-fields $$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)
$$

Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t),$ where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and $u(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for ${x}_{p}(t)$ is given below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from the fact that {{field-1}} matrix.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from line $\text{L5}$ by {{field-2}} both sides of the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ by {{field-3}} both sides of the equation." :question/worked-solution "Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider line $\text{L4}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are solutions to the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ i.e., by substituting any column $c(t)$ of $Φ$ into the homogeneous system, we get

$$
{c}^{′}(t)=Ac(t),
$$

where ${c}^{′}(t)$ is the corresponding column of derivatives in $Φ.$ As a result, this means that ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ.$ Therefore, $\text{L4}$ follows from the fact that $Φ\text{ is a fundamental}$ matrix.

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L5}$ and $\text{L6}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are linearly independent. So, $Φ$ is invertible. Therefore, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by $\text{multiplying by }{Φ}^{-1}$ both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\cdot Φ{u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ ({Φ}^{-1}Φ)\cdot {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ To get $\text{L7},$ we are $\text{integrating}$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L6}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int {Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)\,\text{d}t \\ u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "3e6e22b3-4760-5866-a573-0523c5c9013b" :step/next {:db/id 17592186552559}} {:db/id 17592186552530 :step/content {:db/id 17592186311739 :question/answer-fields "68ae00aa-e57d-5620-9c00-ead6febaac73" :question/math-academy-id "q-336716" :question/problem "Consider the following system of differential equations:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)
$$

Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t),$ where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and $u(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for ${x}_{p}(t)$ is given below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by {{field-1}} both sides of  the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ by {{field-2}} both sides of the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting {{field-3}} into {{field-4}}." :question/worked-solution "Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ To get $\text{L2},$ we are $\text{differentiating}$ with respect to $t$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}^{′}(t) & =(Φu(t))^{′} \\ {x}_{p}^{′}(t) & =Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ To get $\text{L7},$ we are $\text{integrating}$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L6}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int {Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)\,\text{d}t \\ u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L7},$ and $\text{L8}.$ Substituting

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

from $\text{L7}$ into $\text{L1},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φu(t) \\  & =Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L7}$ into $\text{L1}.$"} :step/id #uuid "092c6a00-72eb-562b-a6ec-edba31e0a817"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid {x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}2 & -3 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}x(t)+\overset{f(t)}{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -8\end{bmatrix}}},\,Φ=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & -3{e}^{4t} \\ 0 & 2{e}^{4t}\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the system of differential equations and the fundamental matrix of the corresponding homogeneous system above. Using the method of variation of parameters, compute ${Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)$ and the particular solution ${x}_{p}(t)$ of the system.

</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & -3{e}^{4t} \\ 0 & 2{e}^{4t}\end{bmatrix},\,f(t)=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -8\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{2t}\cdot 2{e}^{4t}-(-3{e}^{4t})\cdot 0}\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{4t} & 3{e}^{4t} \\ 0 & {e}^{2t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-6t}}{2}\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{4t} & 3{e}^{4t} \\ 0 & {e}^{2t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{-2t} & 3{e}^{-2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-4t}\end{bmatrix} \\ {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{-2t} & 3{e}^{-2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-4t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -8\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-10{e}^{-2t} \\ -4{e}^{-4t}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \begin{bmatrix}-10{e}^{-2t} \\ -4{e}^{-4t}\end{bmatrix}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\int -10{e}^{-2t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int -4{e}^{-4t}\,\text{d}t\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5{e}^{-2t} \\ {e}^{-4t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & -3{e}^{4t} \\ 0 & 2{e}^{4t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5{e}^{-2t} \\ {e}^{-4t}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "5095702a-0e43-5e39-ba55-42ec3c14effd" :step/next {:db/id 17592186552603}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "eabf843f-76af-5374-87f3-015cd7c21177" :answer/type {:db/id "77948b35-77f3-58cd-80e2-2c25a0aff174" :question/math-academy-id "q-336705" :question/problem "Consider the following system of differential equations:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)
$$

Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t),$ where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and $u(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for ${x}_{p}(t)$ is given below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}$ into the {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ by {{field-2}} both sides of the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting {{field-3}} into $\text{L1}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L2},$ and $\text{L3}.$ Let's substitute ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$ from $\text{L1}$ and ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$ from $\text{L2}$ into the initial system of ODEs:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =Ax(t)+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t) & =AΦu(t)+f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}$ into $\text{initial system of ODEs}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ To get $\text{L7},$ we are $\text{integrating}$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L6}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int {Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)\,\text{d}t \\ u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L7},$ and $\text{L8}.$ Substituting

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

from $\text{L7}$ into $\text{L1},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φu(t) \\  & =Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L7}$ into $\text{L1}.$"} :step/id #uuid "cc19d89a-a44c-526a-a718-a0cf1438e39d" :step/next {:db/id 17592186552530}} {:answer-field/choices :tutorial/content "Consider the rational equation

$$
\dfrac{12}{x+3} = \dfrac{2}{x-2}.
$$

Recall that when the equation consists of a single rational expression on each side, like the one above, then the easiest way to solve it is usually to use cross-multiplication.

However, before we start, note that $x=-3$ and $x=2$ cannot be solutions. This is because when $x=-3,$ we get a zero in the denominator on the left-hand side, and when $x=2,$ we get a zero in the denominator on the right-hand side.

With this in mind, let's solve the equation. First, we cross-multiply:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{12}{x+3} & =\frac{2}{x-2} \\ 12\cdot (x-2) & =(x+3)\cdot 2 \\ 12x-24 & =2x+6\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we apply the addition and multiplication principles, as usual:

$$
\begin{aligned}12x-24 & =2x+6 \\ 12x-24-2x & =2x+6-2x \\ 10x-24 & =6 \\ 10x-24+24 & =6+24 \\ 10x & =30 \\ \frac{10x}{10} & =\frac{30}{10} \\ x & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Since $x=3$ is different from $x=-3$ and $x=2,$ we accept it as a solution. Thus, the solution is $x=3.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "32ce7197-6c97-5ece-b45d-186993605c4f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8781 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid common factors.

For example, to simplify the rational expression $\dfrac{2x}{2+6x},$ we cancel out a factor of $2$ from the numerator and denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2x}{2+6x} & = \\ \frac{2x}{2(1+3x)} & = \\ \frac{x}{1+3x}\end{aligned}
$$

Sometimes, however, we can have more complicated expressions which require **polynomial factorization** in order to be simplified.

No need to panic though! The main strategy is always the same: factor the numerator and denominator, and then cancel out common factors.

For example, to simplify the rational expression $\dfrac{x^2-4}{x+2},$ we factor the difference of squares in the numerator and then cancel out a common factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}-4}{x+2} & = \\ \frac{(x+2)(x-2)}{x+2} & = \\ \frac{\cancel{(x+2)}(x-2)}{\cancel{x+2}} & = \\ x-2 & \end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "4e98d51f-c45b-52ae-9a50-c3d9b4285aa4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3374 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "df5a03ea-664a-56fe-ac2b-78c919c77b4a" :step/math-academy-id "To add two vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n,$ we just need to add their corresponding components. To illustrate, consider the vectors $\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^4,$ given by

![](images/1f/1f1b79f2e61fccbb27944284cbdd217a311a7f795100cfbb56340a457814b407.svg)

To compute $\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b},$ all we have to do is to add each component of the vector $\mathbf{a}$ with the corresponding component of $\mathbf{b}.$ Doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}a+b & =\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 1 \\ -3 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-5 \\ 3 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5+(-5) \\ 1+3 \\ -3+1 \\ 6+0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 4 \\ -2 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In the Venn diagram, $A\cup B$ is represented by the area that is in either circle (see the illustration below).

![](images/b2/b25a0b74f7b5242f783c38c81bdb4bf8025a847f7079fc90febe510fec041b6d.png)

We count up the outcomes:

- The number of outcomes in $A \cup B$ is
$20+15+25=60$.
- The total number of outcomes in $S$ is
$20+15+25+40=100$.

So, we have

$$
P(A\cup B)=\dfrac{60}{100}= 0.6
$$"} {:db/id 17592186083488 :question/id #uuid "df02e3ef-2a30-5e1b-8976-b1885e4b72ba" :question/math-academy-id "q-11366"} {:db/id 17592186083696 :question/id #uuid "53596b56-3c25-576a-b45e-fe0e8d41745b" :question/math-academy-id "q-42337"} {:db/id 17592186083392 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186082925 :question/id #uuid "fcdd0c3b-36f8-5452-820a-114a8e70aa49" :question/math-academy-id "e-13212"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "c9401702-a2d9-5c53-a3de-8109a75111d7" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186083577 :question/id #uuid "5ab96ff9-7363-5b07-a489-6344524c1799" :question/math-academy-id "q-179553"} {:db/id 17592186083578 :question/id #uuid "d45f3106-f72b-5b34-a881-de8709e0f042" :question/math-academy-id "q-179554"}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing a Probability Given a Description of a Sample Space"} {:db/id 17592186082925 :question/id #uuid "fcdd0c3b-36f8-5452-820a-114a8e70aa49" :question/math-academy-id "e-13212" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186083392 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "c9401702-a2d9-5c53-a3de-8109a75111d7" :knowledge-point/title "Computing a Probability Given a Description of a Sample Space"}] :question/problem "A survey conducted among $100$ students of a music school found that $68$ of them play piano, $39$ of them play violin, and there are $22$ students who play both instruments. - The number of students who play *only* the piano is
$68 - 22 = 46$,
so we write the number $46$ in the part of circle $A$ that does not overlap with circle $B$.
- The number of students who play *only* the violin is
$39 - 22 = 17$,
so we write the number $17$ in the part of the circle $B$ that does not overlap with circle $A$.

The total number of students who play at least one of the instruments is

$$
22+46+17 = 85
$$

and there are $100$ students in total, so the number of remaining students is

$$
100 - 85 = 15
$$

To represent these $15$ students who play neither piano nor violin, we write the number $15$ outside of the circles $A$ and $B$.

Therefore, our Venn diagram looks as shown below:

![](images/cc/cc61c2a5c61467ac19d5debe2c2e53dc48f06f8d153c014f4a73e6feed514900.png)

The shaded part of the Venn diagram corresponds to students who play at least one of the instruments. The probability that a randomly selected student is from this group is given by

$$
P\left(A\cup B\right)=\dfrac{85}{100}= 0.85
$$"} {:db/id 17592186083577 :question/id #uuid "5ab96ff9-7363-5b07-a489-6344524c1799" :question/math-academy-id "q-179553"} {:db/id 17592186083578 :question/id #uuid
