:activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186134047} {:db/id 17592186134619 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135028 :tutorial/content "To construct the standard matrix of a linear transformation $T$ in $\mathbb{R}^2,$ we find the images of the vectors in the standard basis $\{ \mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j} \}$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$ under $T,$ and then use those images as columns in the standard matrix.

To demonstrate, let's consider the following linear transformation: 

![](images/b3/b399f02949935d4a4425b19e4946a3eb47375272bb0271586c93da504ff0bd2e.svg)

Computing $\mathbf T(\mathbf i),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}T(i) & =T\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2\cdot 1-1\cdot 0 \\ 1+3\cdot 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $\mathbf T(\mathbf j),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}T(j) & =T\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2\cdot 0-1\cdot 1 \\ 0+3\cdot 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the standard matrix for this linear transformation is ![](images/be/be0afb6703a6d5e4bcbb360297240a74f4aeec7efbbb1229c8cd01e112fa6bda.svg)

In the diagram below, we see the vectors in the standard basis $\{ \mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j} \}$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and their images $\{ \mathbf{i'}, \mathbf{j'} \}$ under the transformation.

![](images/91/9189a79fe44936221e38e7c051f9f0ddd53338c80cd324ba804d61beef6c2c44.png)

In general, a linear transformation in $\mathbb R^n$ has a standard matrix of dimensions $n \times n,$ whose columns are the images of the basis vectors under the action of the linear transformation." :tutorial/id #uuid "840f3f2c-df1b-50e6-afae-b6c5a434f7a5" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3528 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "5711f04c-b960-52c7-925d-15098acb82c7" :step/math-academy-id 20006 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134622}} {:db/id 17592186135028 :tutorial/content "To construct the standard matrix of a linear transformation $T$ in $\mathbb{R}^2,$ we find the images of the vectors in the standard basis $\{ \mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j} \}$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$ under $T,$ and then use those images as columns in the standard matrix.

$\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle.$ 
A set of vectors 

$$
{U}=\{ \mathbf{u}_1, \cdots, \mathbf{u}_p \}
$$

is called an **orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product** if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal.

For example, let's consider the set

![](images/69/69571997d87ed3f40ee7e9b0742075fbd5ee107892f6a9b4198f75f3f5a9fce3.svg)

and the inner product on $\mathbb{R}^3$ defined as 

$$
\langle \mathbf{x},\mathbf{y} \rangle = x_1 y_1 + 3x_2 y_2 + 2x_3 y_3.
$$

If we denote the vectors in our set ${V}$ as $\{ \mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \mathbf{v}_3 \},$ we can check that ${V}$ is orthogonal by showing that 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}⟨{v}_{1},{v}_{2}⟩=0 \\ ⟨{v}_{1},{v}_{3}⟩=0 \\ ⟨{v}_{2},{v}_{3}⟩=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's compute each inner product:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{v}_{1},{v}_{2}⟩ & =(1)(2)+3(1)(2)+2(1)(-4)=2+6-8=0 & ✓ \\ ⟨{v}_{1},{v}_{3}⟩ & =(1)(-3)+3(1)(1)+2(1)(0)=-3+3+0=0 & ✓ \\ ⟨{v}_{2},{v}_{3}⟩ & =(2)(-3)+3(2)(1)+2(-4)(0)=-6+6+0=0 & ✓\end{aligned}
$$

So indeed, ${V}$ is an orthogonal set." :tutorial/id #uuid "f5f69210-8732-5a94-b16b-b7de520cfc66" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5149 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "30fad2b1-33b1-5011-baca-2c53469ec04d" :question/math-academy-id "q-99827" :question/problem "Consider the following set of functions:

$$
{f}_{1}(t)=1,\,{f}_{2}(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,{f}_{3}(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡2t
$$

Given that the inner product in the vector space $C[-\pi ,\pi ]$ of continuous functions over $[-\pi ,\pi ]$ is defined as 

$$
⟨f(t),g(t)⟩={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(t)g(t)\,\text{d}t,
$$

which of the following statements are true?

I. ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product

II. ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product

:question/math-academy-id "q-99822" :question/problem "Consider the following set of functions:

$$
{f}_{1}(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,{f}_{2}(t)={sin}^{2}⁡t,\,{f}_{3}(t)=1
$$

Given that the inner product in the vector space $C[0,\pi ]$ of continuous functions over $[0,\pi ]$ is defined as 

$$
⟨f(t),g(t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(t)g(t)\,\text{d}t,
$$

which of the following statements are true?

I. ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product

II. ${f}_{2}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product

III. $S=\{{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{3}(t)\}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product

*Hint: $⟨{f}_{1},{f}_{2}⟩=0.$*

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked." :question/worked-solution "Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is called orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{3}(t)⟩ & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,1⟩ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t{|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement II is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{3}(t)⟩=⟨{sin}^{2}⁡t,1⟩={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can evaluate this integral using the identity ${sin}^{2}⁡\alpha =\frac{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\alpha )}{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t))\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[t-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)}{2}]{|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\pi -\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )}{2}-(0-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡0}{2})] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\pi -0-(0-0)] \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{2}(t)⊥̸{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement III is false. Since ${f}_{2}(t)⊥̸{f}_{3}(t),$ the set $S$ is *not* orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only.""} :step/id #uuid "7f2a99f1-09d3-5682-bc31-b6d8c58eeab4" :step/next {:db/id 17592186444799}} {:db/id 17592186444799 :step/content {:db/id 17592186362392 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "7849511c-42aa-5936-80b4-cf27658d9334" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186470002} {:answer/id #uuid "e185f1ae-0f4d-556c-b223-3d5dfc7f46f0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186470003}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186470003} :answer-field/id #uuid "b018c44b-9122-56d8-b47c-5ed9492b1676" :answer-field/key "I" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186470613} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "37fee277-ed91-5718-8df4-97c172646d58" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186470004} {:answer/id #uuid "f141ac45-7382-50ba-b7cb-75b9ede77363" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186470005}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186470005} :answer-field/id #uuid "58c60371-84d6-5ccb-aa0c-f35fe237264d" :answer-field/key "II" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186470614} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6c240535-770a-5ae6-bcc0-9c4deb00ff77" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186470006} {:answer/id #uuid "b1721e3c-52c8-584e-98e8-7fdabdf53653" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186470007}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186470007} :answer-field/id #uuid "b0c46d22-5599-543b-821a-3b2899b69934" :answer-field/key "III" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186470615}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "30fad2b1-33b1-5011-baca-2c53469ec04d" :question/math-academy-id "q-99827" :question/problem "Consider the following set of functions:

$$

$$

which of the following statements are true?

- Statement I is true. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t)⟩ & =⟨t-2,t+2⟩ \\  & =(t-2){|}_{-2}\cdot (t+2){|}_{-2}+(t-2){|}_{2}\cdot (t+2){|}_{2} \\  & =(-2-2)\cdot ((-2)+2)+(2-2)\cdot (2+2) \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${p}_{1}(t)⊥{p}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{3}(t)⟩ & =⟨t-2,2t+4⟩ \\  & =(t-2){|}_{-2}\cdot (2t+4){|}_{-2}+(t-2){|}_{2}\cdot (2t+4){|}_{2} \\  & =(-2-2)\cdot (2(-2)+4)+(2-2)\cdot (2(2)+4) \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${p}_{1}(t)⊥{p}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement III is false. Let's check if ${p}_{2}(t)⊥{p}_{3}(t).$ Computing the inner product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{p}_{2}(t),{p}_{3}(t)⟩ & =⟨t+2,2t+4⟩ \\  & =(t+2){|}_{-2}\cdot (2t+4){|}_{-2}+(t+2){|}_{2}\cdot (2t+4){|}_{2} \\  & =((-2)+2)\cdot (2(-2)+4)+(2+2)\cdot (2(2)+4) \\  & =32\ne 0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${p}_{2}(t)⊥̸{p}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product. So, the set $S$ is *not* an orthogonal set.

$$
{p}_{1}(t)=2t+2,\,{p}_{2}(t)=t-2,\,{p}_{3}(t)=t+1.
$$

Given that the inner product in the vector space ${R}_{1}[t]$ of polynomials of degree at most $1$ in the variable $t$ is defined as 

$$
⟨p(t),q(t)⟩=p(-1)q(-1)+p(2)q(2),
$$

which of the following statements are true?

I. ${p}_{1}(t)⊥{p}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product

II. ${p}_{2}(t)⊥̸{p}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product

III. $S=\{{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t),{p}_{3}(t)\}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked." :question/worked-solution "Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t)⟩ & =⟨2t+2,t-2⟩ \\  & =(2t+2){|}_{-1}\cdot (t-2){|}_{-1}+(2t+2){|}_{2}\cdot (t-2){|}_{2} \\  & =(2(-1)+2)\cdot ((-1)-2)+(2(2)+2)\cdot (2-2) \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${p}_{1}(t)⊥{p}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement II is false since

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{p}_{2}(t),{p}_{3}(t)⟩ & =⟨t-2,t+1⟩ \\  & =(t-2){|}_{-1}\cdot (t+1){|}_{-1}+(t-2){|}_{2}\cdot (t+1){|}_{2} \\  & =((-1)-2)\cdot ((-1)+1)+(2-2)\cdot (2+1) \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${p}_{2}(t)⊥{p}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement III is false. Let's check if ${p}_{1}(t)⊥{p}_{3}(t).$ Computing the inner product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{3}(t)⟩ & =⟨2t+2,t+1⟩ \\  & =(2t+2){|}_{-1}\cdot (t+1){|}_{-1}+(2t+2){|}_{2}\cdot (t+1){|}_{2} \\  & =(2(-1)+2)\cdot ((-1)+1)+(2(2)+2)\cdot (2+1) \\  & =18\ne 0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${p}_{1}(t)⊥̸{p}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product. So, the set $S$ is *not* an orthogonal set.

"q-99656" :question/problem "$$
{v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix},\,{v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{v}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the vectors shown above. Given that the inner product in the vector space ${R}^{3}$ is defined as 

$$
⟨x,y⟩={x}_{1}{y}_{1}+2{x}_{2}{y}_{2}+2{x}_{3}{y}_{3},
$$

which of the following statements are true?
- **I.** ${v}_{1}⊥{v}_{2}$ with respect to the given inner product
- **II.** ${v}_{2}⊥̸{v}_{3}$ with respect to the given inner product
- **III.** $S={{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked." :question/worked-solution "Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{v}_{1},{v}_{2}⟩ & =(1)(4)+2(1)(-1)+2(-1)(1) \\  & =4-2-2 \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${v}_{1}⊥{v}_{2}$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement II is false since 

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{v}_{2},{v}_{3}⟩ & =(4)(0)+2(-1)(1)+2(1)(1) \\  & =0-2+2 \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${v}_{2}⊥{v}_{3}$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement III is true. Indeed, computing the inner product $⟨{v}_{1},{v}_{3}⟩$, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{v}_{1},{v}_{3}⟩ & =(1)(0)+2(1)(1)+2(-1)(1) \\  & =0+2-2 \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${v}_{1}⊥{v}_{3}$ with respect to the given inner product.
As a result, the set $S$ is orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only.""} :step/id #uuid "068d6b66-d519-5161-9eb3-7efaee833625" :step/next {:db/id 17592186518316}} {:db/id 17592186518233 :step/content {:db/id 17592186362397 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "b37083a7-aaaa-5a2a-973a-5c9ff944dfe5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186470032} {:answer/id #uuid "aade6615-cdec-5bb3-9ebc-b52ba6498acb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186470033}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186470033} :answer-field/id #uuid "8ee6465c-b492-5dcd-9a5b-72f46a3a5104" :answer-field/key "I" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186470628} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8dcfb967-51e5-5257-b6ea-f6b21931da14" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186470034} {:answer/id #uuid "d6927137-4c46-5fd0-a3de-bc83e11cc13a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186470035}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186470034} :answer-field/id #uuid "f55811ff-e66f-5a0e-812a-3b75349cc59e" :answer-field/key "II" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186470629} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1ec93396-6ade-5b54-b2dc-4c3f0308a1a8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186470036} {:answer/id #uuid "42e1db1a-4eb1-5170-b19b-b7d378bf5855" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186470037}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186470036} :answer-field/id #uuid "8547b10e-8dd7-5314-9138-e70dea301350" :answer-field/key "III" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186470630}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "d313e454-e9a2-5532-b1b1-37c4d7cbbe80" :question/math-academy-id "q-99951" :question/problem "Consider the following set of functions:

- Statement I is false. We have

\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can evaluate this integral using the identity $\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ))$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+t))\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t))\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)){|}_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}))-\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{4}{3}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot (-\frac{4}{3}) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement II is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{3}(t)⟩=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}{sin}^{2}⁡t{|}_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-{sin}^{2}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(1-1) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{2}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement III is false. Since ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{2}(t),$ the set $S$ is *not* orthogonal.

Given that the inner product in the vector space $C[-1,1]$ of continuous functions over $[-1,1]$ is defined as 

$$
⟨f(t),g(t)⟩={\int }_{-1}^{1}f(t)g(t)\,\text{d}t,
$$

which of the following statements are true?

I. ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product

*Hint: $⟨{f}_{1},{f}_{3}⟩=0.$*" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is called orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩ & =⟨{t}^{2},{t}^{3}⟩ \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{t}^{2}\cdot {t}^{3}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{t}^{5}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{{t}^{6}}{6}{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =\frac{{1}^{6}}{6}-\frac{(-1)^{6}}{6} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement II is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{3}(t)⟩ & =⟨{t}^{3},t⟩ \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{t}^{3}\cdot t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{t}^{4}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{{t}^{5}}{5}{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =\frac{{1}^{5}}{5}-\frac{(-1)^{5}}{5} \\  & =\frac{2}{5}\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{2}(t)⊥̸{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement III is false. Since ${f}_{2}(t)⊥̸{f}_{3}(t),$ the set $S$ is *not* orthogonal.

$$

We can evaluate this integral using the identity $\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ))$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+t))\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t))\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)){|}_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}))-\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{4}{3}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot (-\frac{4}{3}) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement II is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{3}(t)⟩=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

This means that ${f}_{2}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

:topic/math-academy-id 2168} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186134701 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135061 :tutorial/content "Let's consider the least-squares problem for the system

$$
A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}.
$$

We can use QR factorization to construct the least-squares solution of this system. Recall that finding the QR factorization of $A$ means expressing $A$ in the form

$$
A = QR,
$$

where

- $Q$ has orthonormal columns, and

- $R$ is an upper triangular matrix with positive entries on its main diagonal.

To see how QR factorization can be used to solve a least-squares problem, we first recall that the least-squares solution satisfies the normal equation

$$
A^T A \mathbf{x} = A^T \mathbf{b}.
$$

Substituting $A = QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, we have $Q^T Q = I.$ Therefore, the above equation becomes

$$
R^TR\mathbf{x} = R^TQ^T\mathbf{b}.
$$

Since $R^T$ is invertible, pre-multiplying our equation by $(R^T)^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b\end{aligned}
$$

which simplifies as

$$
R \mathbf{x} = Q^T \mathbf{b}.  \qquad\qquad (\ast)
$$

The least-squares solution $\hat{\mathbf x}$ can now be found by solving this equation using back-substitution or row operations. This is usually the fastest way.

If we want an explicit formula for the least-squares solution, then we note that since $R$ is invertible, pre-multiplying $(\ast)$ by $R^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{R}^{-1}\cdot Rx & ={R}^{-1}\cdot {Q}^{T}b\end{aligned}
$$

which simplifies as

$$
\mathbf{x} = R^{-1} Q^T \mathbf{b}.
$$

The least-squares solution is unique if $A$ has linearly independent columns." :tutorial/id #uuid "7a9501fc-fdbc-5905-ad31-e3c6c2767a33" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3639 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} $$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}3\sqrt{2}{x}_{1}-4\sqrt{2}{x}_{2} &=38\sqrt{2} \\ 2{x}_{2} &=-10.\end{aligned}\right.

$$

- The eigenvalues of $A$ are all real.

- The eigenvectors corresponding to *different* eigenvalues are orthogonal.

- The dimension of the eigenspace for each eigenvalue equals the multiplicity of that eigenvalue as a root of the characteristic polynomial.

Specifically, if $\mathbf{u}_i$ denotes an orthonormal eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda_i$ for $i=1,\ldots, n$, then

$$
A=\sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i \mathbf{u}_i \mathbf{u}_i^T.
$$

Expressing a symmetric matrix $A$ in this way is called the **spectral decomposition** of $A.$

To demonstrate, let's find the spectral decomposition of the $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A,$ given by

![](images/40/408e7471e4ef788758d423af97f5683186f79192fd8933c350d45bb87f089875.svg)

The eigenvalues of $A$ are $\lambda_1 = 6$ and $\lambda_2 = -4,$ and the corresponding eigenvectors are

![](images/0c/0c22f7dd97e83c358cb3cef1fcc2db902d908140109334a8cf1c22b35b29c6d2.svg)

The spectral decomposition of $A$ is given by

$$
A =\sum_{i=1}^2 \lambda_i \mathbf{u}_i \mathbf{u}_i^T = \lambda_1 \mathbf u_1 \mathbf u_1^T + \lambda_2 \mathbf u_2 \mathbf u_2^T,
$$

where $\mathbf u_1$ and $\mathbf u_2$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2,$ respectively.

First, let's normalize our eigenvectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\ {u}_{2} & =\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the spectral decomposition of $A$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}{u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}{u}_{2}^{T} \\  & =6\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3\end{bmatrix}+(-4)\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =6\cdot \frac{1}{10}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 & 3\end{bmatrix}+(-4)\cdot \frac{1}{10}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}3 & -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={{6}_{⏟}}_{{\lambda }_{1}}\cdot {{\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{10} & \frac{3}{10} \\ \frac{3}{10} & \frac{9}{10}\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{u}_{1}{u}_{1}^{T}}+{{(-4)}_{⏟}}_{{\lambda }_{2}}\cdot {{\begin{bmatrix}\frac{9}{10} & -\frac{3}{10} \\ -\frac{3}{10} & \frac{1}{10}\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{u}_{2}{u}_{2}^{T}}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this decomposition, the matrix $\mathbf{u}_i \mathbf{u}_i^T$ is the orthogonal projection matrix that maps any $\mathbf x \in \mathbb R^2$ onto the subspace spanned by $\mathbf u_i.$" :tutorial/id Moreover, ${u}_{i}\cdot {u}_{i}^{T}$ is the projection matrix corresponding to ${u}_{i}.$

First, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda =2.$ Computing $A-2I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & -4 \\ -4 & 18\end{bmatrix}-2\begin{bmatrix}1 & -4 \\ -4 & 16\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -4 \\ -4 & 16\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -4 & 0 \\ -4 & 16 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$
v=\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot {u}^{T} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{17}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}4 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{17}\begin{bmatrix}16 & 4 \\ 4 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively.

Moreover, ${u}_{i}\cdot {u}_{i}^{T}$ is the projection matrix corresponding to ${u}_{i}.$

First, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda =1.$ Computing $A-1I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =\begin{bmatrix}10 & 12 \\ 12 & 17\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}9 & 12 \\ 12 & 16\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}9 & 12 & 0 \\ 12 & 16 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{4}{3}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}9 & 12 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-\frac{4}{3}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{4}{3}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=3,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix},
$$

$$
u=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot {u}^{T} & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{25}\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-4 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{25}\begin{bmatrix}16 & -12 \\ -12 & 9\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

$$

symmetric matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}^{T},
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively.

Moreover, ${u}_{i}\cdot {u}_{i}^{T}$ is the projection matrix corresponding to ${u}_{i}.$

First, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda =4.$ Computing $A-4I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 6 \\ 6 & 0\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-9 & 6 \\ 6 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-9 & 6 & 0 \\ 6 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(\frac{2}{3}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-9 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=\frac{2}{3}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=3,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖v‖=\sqrt{13}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm, we obtain the normalized eigenvector: 

$$
u=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, the required orthogonal projection matrix is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot {u}^{T} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}2 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{13}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{13}[\begin{aligned}4 & 6 \\ 6 & 9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "f8df9c63-69f3-5acb-8e84-5b34d208def1"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3a0018a6-7dae-54cf-88b4-02338b8fff5b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "q-140844" :question/problem "Given that $A$ is a $4\times 4$ real symmetric matrix, which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $A$ is not diagonalizable
- **II.** $A$ must have $4$ integer eigenvalues
- **III.** If  $\alpha $ is an eigenvalue of $A$ with the multiplicity $2,$ then the dimension of the eigenspace for the eigenvalue $\alpha $ is $2.$" :question/worked-solution "Given that $A$ is an $n\times n$ symmetric matrix over $R$, the spectral theorem states the following:

- The eigenvalues of $A$ are all real.

- Eigenvectors corresponding to different eigenvalues are orthogonal.

- The dimension of the eigenspace for each eigenvalue equals the multiplicity of that eigenvalue as a root of the characteristic polynomial.

- $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. According to the spectral theorem, any symmetric matrix with real entries is orthogonally diagonalizable, so, $A$ is diagonalizable.

- Statement II is false. According to the spectral theorem, the eigenvalues are real but not necessarily integers.

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively.

Moreover, ${u}_{i}\cdot {u}_{i}^{T}$ is the projection matrix corresponding to ${u}_{i}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =\begin{bmatrix}-15 & 12 \\ 12 & -8\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-16 & 12 \\ 12 & -9\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}-16 & 12 & 0 \\ 12 & -9 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{3}{4}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-16 & 12 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$
v=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 4\end{bmatrix},

$$
u=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot {u}^{T} & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{25}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}3 & 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{25}\begin{bmatrix}9 & 12 \\ 12 & 16\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

How can we find the intersection point $P$ of $l$ and $\Pi?$

We start by writing the equation of the line in the form $\mathbf{r} = \langle 2+3t , 2, 1+t \rangle.$ Now, since $P$ must lie on the line $l,$ we can write its coordinates as $P(2+3t , 2, 1+t)$ for some particular value of $t \in (-\infty,\infty).$

![](images/d3/d3ba164eb98a53c463744e11d6593177ddde2a0a309f752e5d86b30db0d79925.png)

On the other hand, $P$ also lies on the plane $\Pi.$ So, the coordinates $P(2+3t , 2, 1+t)$ must satisfy the equation of the plane as well. Substituting the position vector $\mathbf{r} = \langle 2+3t , 2, 1+t \rangle$ into the equation of the plane and solving for $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r\cdot ⟨3,-5,1⟩ & =7 \\ ⟨2+3t,2,1+t⟩\cdot ⟨3,-5,1⟩ & =7 \\ 3(2+3t)-5\cdot 2+(1+t) & =7 \\ 6+9t-10+1+t & =7 \\ 10t & =10 \\ t & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

To get the position vector $\mathbf{p}$ of the intersection point $P,$ we substitute $t=1$ into the equation of the line:

$$
\begin{aligned}p & =⟨2+3(1),2,1+(1)⟩ \\  & =⟨5,2,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

:question/math-academy-id "q-74004" :question/problem "Find the intersection point of the line $l$ and the plane $Π$ with equations

$$
l:r=⟨3,1,5⟩+w⟨-2,-5,4⟩,\,Π:r=⟨-5,4,2⟩+s⟨0,3,1⟩+t⟨2,0,1⟩.
$$" :question/worked-solution "From the equation of a plane in the parametric form $r=p+tv+sw$, we have that its normal vector is $n=v\times w.$ In our case, the normal vectors to $Π$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =v\times w \\  & =⟨0,3,1⟩\times ⟨2,0,1⟩ \\  & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}|k \\  & =3i+2j-6k \\  & =⟨3,2,-6⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the plane $Π$ in dot product form is

$$
\begin{aligned}r\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ r\cdot ⟨3,2,-6⟩ & =⟨-5,4,2⟩\cdot ⟨3,2,-6⟩ \\ r\cdot ⟨3,2,-6⟩ & =-19.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $r=⟨3,1,5⟩+w⟨-2,-5,4⟩$ into the equation of the plane in dot product form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r\cdot ⟨3,2,-6⟩ & =-19 \\ ⟨3-2w,1-5w,5+4w⟩\cdot ⟨3,2,-6⟩ & =-19 \\ 3(3-2w)+2(1-5w)-6(5+4w) & =-19 \\ 9-6w+2-10w-30-24w & =-19 \\ -40w & =0 \\ w & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to get the position vector $q$ of the intersection point $Q,$ we substitute $w=0$ into the equation of the line:

$$
\begin{aligned}q & =⟨3-2(0),1-5(0),5+4(0)⟩ \\  & =⟨3,1,5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, the intersection point is $Q(3,1,5).$"} :step/id #uuid "0227058d-e862-5e31-b5c8-bea4849a37b5" :step/next {:db/id 17592186484327}} {:db/id 17592186484313 :step/content {:db/id 17592186342127 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1b2ccf68-fbc4-58ea-80f0-c47a1f4e61c5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "No intersection" :db/id 17592186339365} {:answer/id #uuid "1d364631-26c0-59a4-93c9-0842ba8027a4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(19,10,16)" :db/id 17592186339381} {:answer/id #uuid "2bfe2f6a-4b05-5041-9be9-ec95d41ced84" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(18,8,12)" :db/id 17592186339510} {:answer/id #uuid "90fc5ea2-94e0-5824-91af-e274368bde07" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(18,11,16)" :db/id 17592186340429} {:answer/id #uuid "a5f82de1-4dec-5d15-9285-344580d1aa1f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(8,-1,6)" :db/id 17592186340633}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186340429} :answer-field/id #uuid "3769c405-5ffb-59ea-8180-d6fbf6837b56" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186341479}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "8a17e320-306c-50fa-b84b-f8cbe958e629" :question/math-academy-id "q-73993" :question/problem "Find the intersection point of the line $l$ and the plane $Π$ with equations

$$" :question/worked-solution "We can substitute the parametric expressions for $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ of the line into the equation of the plane immediately:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+5y-8z & =186 \\ 2(8+3t)+5(-6+7t)-8(2t) & =186 \\ 16+6t-30+35t-16t & =186 \\ 25t & =200 \\ t & =8\end{aligned}
$$

To get the position vector $p$ of the intersection point $P$, we substitute $t=8$ into the parametric equations of the line:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=8+3(8)=32 \\ y &=-6+7(8)=50 \\ z &=2(8)=16\end{aligned}\right.
$$

$$
l:r=⟨-5,0,1⟩+t⟨-3,1,0⟩,\,Π:-3x+y-2z+27=0.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Let's start by writing the equation of the line as

$$
r=⟨-5-3t,t,1⟩.

Let's also write the equation of the plane in the dot product form:

$$
\begin{aligned}-3x+y-2z+27 & =0 \\ -3x+y-2z & =-27 \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot ⟨-3,1,-2⟩ & =-27 \\ r\cdot ⟨-3,1,-2⟩ & =-27\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $r=⟨-5-3t,t,1⟩$ into the equation of the plane, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r\cdot ⟨-3,1,-2⟩ & =-27 \\ ⟨-5-3t,t,1⟩\cdot ⟨-3,1,-2⟩ & =-27 \\ -3(-5-3t)+1\cdot t-2\cdot 1 & =-27 \\ 15+9t+t-2 & =-27 \\ 10t & =-40 \\ t & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to get the position vector $p$ of the intersection point $P,$ we substitute $t=-4$ into the equation of the line:

$$
\begin{aligned}p & =⟨-5-3(-4),-4,1⟩ \\  & =⟨7,-4,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the intersection point is $P(7,-4,1).$"} :step/id #uuid "5afd2fb8-f672-52e7-a18b-c486687e5ed6" :step/next {:db/id 17592186516948}} {:db/id 17592186516916 :step/content {:db/id 17592186515570 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0a4e4e53-6530-5d9b-ac71-88fa4a852643" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(7,5,12)" :db/id 17592186514894} {:answer/id #uuid "13d7977a-6ece-5a3d-a4d3-a046ae5ee70a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(4,3,8)" :db/id 17592186514914} {:answer/id #uuid "3e792c4b-0f89-58e4-ad54-bf65b7f20967" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "No intersection" :db/id 17592186515006} {:answer/id #uuid "97dcbf66-8c48-507d-96c6-a848577b2e92" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-5,-3,-4)" :db/id 17592186515192} {:answer/id #uuid "a9993b57-a418-5d19-be94-6b1c3a3b00c8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(8,5,8)" :db/id 17592186515229}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186514914} :answer-field/id #uuid "c8d9ffbc-23ef-519d-9512-884d3bb1903d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186515494}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "83aacc67-1785-59c3-94ae-6f65bea01fe4" :question/math-academy-id "q-108881" :question/problem "Find the intersection point of the line $l$ and the plane $Π$ with equations

$$
l:\frac{x+2}{3}=\frac{y+1}{2}=\frac{z}{4},\,Π:r\cdot ⟨3,-1,2⟩=25.
$$" :question/worked-solution "From the equation of the line $l$, we know that it passes through the point $A(-2,-1,0)$ and it is parallel to the vector $v=⟨3,2,4⟩.$ Therefore, its vector equation is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨-2,-1,0⟩+t⟨3,2,4⟩ \\  & =⟨-2+3t,-1+2t,4t⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Now, substituting $r=⟨-2+3t,-1+2t,4t⟩$ into the equation of the plane, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r\cdot ⟨3,-1,2⟩ & =25 \\ ⟨-2+3t,-1+2t,4t⟩\cdot ⟨3,-1,2⟩ & =25 \\ 3(-2+3t)-(-1+2t)+2(4t) & =25 \\ -6+9t+1-2t+8t & =25 \\ 15t & =30 \\ t & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to get the position vector $p$ of the intersection point $P,$ we substitute $t=2$ into the equation of the line:

$$
\begin{aligned}p & =⟨-2+3(2),-1+2(2),4(2)⟩ \\  & =⟨4,3,8⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get $P(4,3,8).$"} :step/id #uuid "6b2e7866-b57f-55d0-8fca-843a70bc51a0"} {:db/id 17592186516919 :step/content {:db/id 17592186516797 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "58a61e2d-79ec-5942-a542-a599506c947f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(2,8,4)" :db/id 17592186516299} {:answer/id #uuid "5933b3cc-3b81-55f6-a9e9-d8ce70b49ee7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(6,-4,1)" :db/id 17592186516303} {:answer/id #uuid "8c3399b1-2e8d-5048-9705-3b903a795275" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "No intersection" :db/id 17592186516404} {:answer/id #uuid "be96b637-0ffd-5d98-b663-5c2fe316eeca" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(6,-4,-16)" :db/id 17592186516515} {:answer/id #uuid "f5f1cb12-78bd-54f6-9673-719b825438c6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(3,5,-1)" :db/id 17592186516624}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186516299} :answer-field/id #uuid "96cd3fdc-919f-5a7e-9267-58831d9b0de1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186516725}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "47b66d2c-d386-5a47-ab3a-e7307c9bb3f9" :question/math-academy-id "q-108335" :question/problem "Find the intersection point of the line $l$ and the plane $Π$ with equations

:topic/id #uuid "36128875-8025-5e37-8397-54d8247d47c9" :topic/math-academy-id 3131} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186163048 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163315 :tutorial/content "Let's suppose we are given the matrix

![](images/18/18f57c05cb79918e17401427e3419648791562a5d38116582e0d396e20db1069.svg)

Then, the corresponding linear transformation 

$$
\mathbf x \mapsto A \mathbf x
$$

maps the unit circle $\big\{ \mathbf x \, | \, \|\mathbf x\|=1 \big\}$ in $\mathbb R^2$ onto an ellipse $\big\{ A\mathbf{x} \,|\, \| \mathbf{x} \| =1 \big\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^2,$ as shown below. 

![](images/c1/c163f7714d0e2045db37438b7ea66a2dc8ac92cfbe309a0d24c898bbfac8c295.png)

 

How can we find the maximum possible value of $\|A \mathbf x\|?$ Geometrically, this is equivalent to finding the semi-major axis of our ellipse.

![](images/86/866052291b0d7a416988c0c42fa99eec1d1bfd3b1344cf3cf2eb0a09457ae38d.png)

First, we note the following:

- The value of $\mathbf x$ that maximizes $||A\mathbf x||$ also maximizes $||A\mathbf x||^2.$

- If $\mathbf v$ is a column vector, then $||\mathbf v||^2 = \mathbf v^T \mathbf v\mathbin{:}$

Therefore, we can re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $A\mathbf{x}$ on our ellipse as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x\end{aligned}
$$

  

Note that $\mathbf{x}^T (A^T A) \mathbf{x}$ is a quadratic form with the matrix $A^T A.$ Therefore, the maximum value of this quadratic form for $\| \mathbf{x} \| =1$ equals the largest eigenvalue of the matrix $A^T A.$

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}10 & 6 \\ 6 & 10\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^TA\mathbin{:}$  

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}10-\lambda  & 6 \\ 6 & 10-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (10-\lambda )^{2}-36 & =0 \\ (10-\lambda )^{2} & =36 \\ 10-\lambda  & =\pm 6 \\ \lambda  & =4,\,16\end{aligned}
$$

Since the largest eigenvalue of $A^T A$ is $16,$ we obtain

$$
\max\limits_{\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1} \big\{ \| A\mathbf{x} \|^2 \big\} = 16
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\max\limits_{\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1} \big\{ \| A\mathbf{x} \| \big\} = \sqrt{16} = 4.
$$

 

Therefore, the length of the semi-major axis of our ellipse equals $4.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b6f73158-b78c-5262-bb9d-a957e3f79fa3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6133 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} 17592186163050}} {:db/id 17592186163052 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163316 :tutorial/content "Let $A$ be an $m\times n$ matrix. Then, $A^T A$ is always a symmetric, positive semi-definite matrix. In particular, $A^TA$ can be orthogonally diagonalized, and its eigenvalues are non-negative real numbers.

The **singular values** of  $A$ are defined as the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^T A.$ The $i$th singular value of $A$ is denoted $\sigma_i\mathbin{:}$

- $\sigma_1 = \sqrt{\lambda_1}$

- $\sigma_2 = \sqrt{\lambda_2}$

- $\sigma_3 = \sqrt{\lambda_3}$

$\:\vdots$

- $\sigma_n = \sqrt{\lambda_n}$

We usually list the singular values in *decreasing* order. 

Now, we know that $A^TA$ is orthogonally diagonalizable. Therefore, if

$$
\left\{\mathbf v_1, \mathbf v_2\,\ldots, \mathbf v_n\right\}
$$

is an *orthonormal* basis of $\mathbb R^n$ consisting of the eigenvectors of ${A^T}{A}$ with the corresponding eigenvalues 

$$
\lambda_1\geq \lambda_2\geq \ldots \geq \lambda_n,
$$

then it can be shown that

- $\sigma_1 = \sqrt{\lambda_1}$ is the length of $A\mathbf v_1,$

- $\sigma_2 = \sqrt{\lambda_2}$ is the length of $A\mathbf v_2,$

$\:\vdots$

- $\sigma_n = \sqrt{\lambda_n}$ is the length of $A\mathbf v_n.$

Furthermore:

- $\sigma_1$ is the maximum value of $||A\mathbf x||$ over all *unit* vectors $\mathbf x,$ and is attained on the unit eigenvector $\mathbf v_1$

- $\sigma_2$ is the maximum value of $||A\mathbf x||$ over all *unit* vectors $\mathbf x$ that are orthogonal to $\mathbf v_1,$ and is attained on the unit eigenvector $\mathbf v_2$

- $\sigma_3$ is the maximum value of $||A\mathbf x||$ over all *unit* vectors $\mathbf x$ that are orthogonal to $\mathbf v_1$ *and* $\mathbf v_2,$ and is attained on the unit eigenvector $\mathbf v_3$

$\:\vdots$

- $\sigma_n$ is the maximum value of $||A\mathbf x||$ over all *unit* vectors $\mathbf x$ that are orthogonal to $\mathbf v_1,\mathbf v_2,\ldots,\mathbf v_{n-1},$ and is attained on the unit eigenvector $\mathbf v_n$

Let's take a look at a concrete example." :tutorial/id #uuid "f470bdb6-fa79-595c-beba-f8242d4426bd" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6134 :tutorial/title "The Singular Values of a Matrix"} :step/id #uuid "ef1b9251-7972-5caa-8ac8-321830fa4c27" :step/math-academy-id 37255 :step/next {:db/id 17592186163056}} {:db/id 17592186163056 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163320 :tutorial/content "We've seen that for the matrix $A,$ given by

![](images/9c/9c11e176876a767543250d5b18038cae7b14a36a692a6f14474da6b4312a48b9.svg)

the eigenvalues of $A^TA$ are $\lambda_1=16$ and $\lambda_2=4.$ It's easy to show that the corresponding unit eigenvectors of $A^T A$ are 

![](images/7c/7c44b67b766ea8385f4d7780523ee560bd3e215a0cee42db9baf208da471ccdd.svg) 

The singular values of $A$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{16}=4, \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{4}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Putting all of this information together gives us the following diagram. 

![](images/23/238f4ae60c783dd786476a339f012ef1b4ca82bcac7aa3f3ef4445726938ef3a.png)

 

Note that our ellipse's semi-major and semi-minor axes are $\sigma_1 = 4$ and $\sigma_2 =2,$ respectively." :tutorial/id #uuid "a319c696-fd06-5e8f-99f1-26ad08271a27" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6139 :tutorial/title "Associating Singular Values With an Ellipse's Principal Axes"} :step/id #uuid "c9015782-c2cb-5d34-8e6d-84a7dd5678d9" :step/math-academy-id 37280 :step/next {:db/id 17592186163051}}] :activity/title "The Singular Values of a Matrix" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186162225} {:db/id 17592186163048 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163315 :tutorial/content "Let's suppose we are given the matrix

Then, $A^T A$ is always a symmetric, positive semi-definite matrix. In particular, $A^TA$ can be orthogonally diagonalized, and its eigenvalues are non-negative real numbers.

The **singular values** of  $A$ are defined as the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^T A.$ The $i$th singular value of $A$ is denoted $\sigma_i\mathbin{:}$

- $\sigma_1 = \sqrt{\lambda_1}$

- $\sigma_2 = \sqrt{\lambda_2}$

- $\sigma_3 = \sqrt{\lambda_3}$

$\:\vdots$

- $\sigma_n = \sqrt{\lambda_n}$

We usually list the singular values in *decreasing* order. 

Now, we know that $A^TA$ is orthogonally diagonalizable. Therefore, if

$$
\left\{\mathbf v_1, \mathbf v_2\,\ldots, \mathbf v_n\right\}
$$

is an *orthonormal* basis of $\mathbb R^n$ consisting of the eigenvectors of ${A^T}{A}$ with the corresponding eigenvalues 

$$

- $\sigma_1 = \sqrt{\lambda_1}$ is the length of $A\mathbf v_1,$

- $\sigma_2 = \sqrt{\lambda_2}$ is the length of $A\mathbf v_2,$

$\:\vdots$

- $\sigma_n = \sqrt{\lambda_n}$ is the length of $A\mathbf v_n.$

Furthermore:

- $\sigma_1$ is the maximum value of $||A\mathbf x||$ over all *unit* vectors $\mathbf x,$ and is attained on the unit eigenvector $\mathbf v_1$

- $\sigma_2$ is the maximum value of $||A\mathbf x||$ over all *unit* vectors $\mathbf x$ that are orthogonal to $\mathbf v_1,$ and is attained on the unit eigenvector $\mathbf v_2$

- $\sigma_n$ is the maximum value of $||A\mathbf x||$ over all *unit* vectors $\mathbf x$ that are orthogonal to $\mathbf v_1,\mathbf v_2,\ldots,\mathbf v_{n-1},$ and is attained on the unit eigenvector $\mathbf v_n$

length of the semi-major axis of the ellipse." :question/worked-solution "The matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{3}$ onto the ellipse $\{Ax\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ in ${R}^{2}.$

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $Ax$ on our ellipse, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x,\end{aligned}
$$

  

where ${x}^{T}({A}^{T}A)x$ is the quadratic form with the symmetric matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The square roots of the eigenvalues of ${A}^{T}A$ are called the *singular values* of $A.$ Since the largest singular value of $A$ is ${\sigma }_{1}=12,$ the largest eigenvalue of ${A}^{T}A$ must be ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}={12}^{2}.$ So, we obtain that

$$
{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax{‖}^{2}\}={12}^{2}\,⟹\,{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax‖\}=12.
$$

 

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is ${\sigma }_{1}=12.$"} :step/id #uuid "410ad0cd-66aa-589e-9d24-b7c90f23a34c" :step/next {:db/id 17592186503797}} {:db/id 17592186503786 :step/content {:db/id 17592186162363 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "27612a52-9a44-5194-990a-b67bd5b0cb3c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{v}_{1}" :db/id 17592186266495} {:answer/id #uuid "3781afe7-ca23-5caf-8d77-e210ce87765d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "7" :db/id 17592186266623} {:answer/id #uuid "9cbfef3a-23de-5494-b267-533971519fee" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186267552} {:answer/id #uuid "a48b2a55-e19f-5a3b-aad5-9311f9e9ad3f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{v}_{2}" :db/id 17592186267628} {:answer/id #uuid "a9e9b4e6-ef6f-5008-83b9-4dc476b26261" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "7{v}_{1}+5{v}_{2}" :db/id 17592186267677}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186267628} :answer-field/id #uuid "4f73eb28-9edf-5454-bbc8-1e8090f60bd5" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186268549}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "14414eae-18ed-5455-a3d4-1f9724606970" :question/math-academy-id "q-139421" :question/problem "![](images/f2/f26e876d5234313926a2cbaa8938e32c8a725cf3435ce3113361bfa3dc1b7997.png)

17592186134817 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135105 :tutorial/content "Let $V$ be an inner product space with the inner product $\langle\cdot, \cdot\rangle.$ If 

$$
\big\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 , \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n \big\}
$$

 is a set of mutually orthogonal vectors in $V,$  then the **orthogonal projection** of a vector $\mathbf{x}\in V$ onto the subspace 

$$
S = \textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 , \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n \}
$$

with respect to the inner product is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x+⋯+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{n}}x \\  & =\frac{⟨x,{a}_{1}⟩}{⟨{a}_{1},{a}_{1}⟩}{a}_{1}+\frac{⟨x,{a}_{2}⟩}{⟨{a}_{2},{a}_{2}⟩}{a}_{2}+⋯+\frac{⟨x,{a}_{n}⟩}{⟨{a}_{n},{a}_{n}⟩}{a}_{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto $S$ is the sum of the orthogonal projections of $\mathbf{x}$ onto each one-dimensional subspace $\textrm{Span}\big\{ \mathbf{a}_i\}$ for $i=1, 2, \cdots, n.$ 

Note the following:

- This is entirely analogous to the corresponding formula for Euclidean spaces.

- As in Euclidean spaces, the formula works *only* when the set of vectors $\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 , \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n \}$ is orthogonal with respect to the inner product!" :tutorial/id "e60ded4d-fa5d-5393-8f16-7c1cc6abe2dd" :step/math-academy-id 32459 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134820}} {:db/id 17592186134820 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135106 :tutorial/content "Suppose that $V$ is a vector space equipped with an inner product $\left\langle\cdot, \cdot\right\rangle$ and that $\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{w} \in V.$ The **distance $d$ between $\mathbf v$ and $\mathbf w$ with respect to the inner product** is defined by the *norm* of $\mathbf{v}- \mathbf{w}.$ That is,

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =‖v-w‖=\sqrt{⟨v-w,v-w⟩}.\end{aligned}
$$

For example, suppose that $V = \mathcal{C}[0,1],$ the vector space of continuous functions over $[0,1],$ equipped with the inner product

$$
\langle x(t),y(t) \rangle = \int_0^{1} x(t) y(t) \, \text{d}t.
$$

The distance between the functions $f(t)=4t$ and $g(t)=t+1$ with respect to the given inner product is

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =‖f(t)-g(t)‖ \\  & =‖4t-(t+1)‖ \\  & =‖3t-1‖ \\  & =\sqrt{⟨3t-1,3t-1⟩} \\  & =\sqrt{{\int }_{0}^{1}(3t-1)^{2}\,\text{d}t} \\  & =\sqrt{{\frac{1}{9}\cdot (3t-1)^{3}|}_{0}^{1}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{9}\cdot [(8)-(-1)]} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{9}\cdot 9} \\  & =\sqrt{1} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

More generally, given an orthogonal set 

$$
\big\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 , \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n \big\} \subset  V
$$

and a vector $\mathbf x \in V,$  the **distance between $\mathbf{x}$ and the subspace** 

$$
S=\textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2,  \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n \}
$$

is defined as

$$
\Vert{ \color{black} \mathbf{x} - \text{proj}_{S}\,\mathbf{x} }\Vert.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "4ca26c36-a2e4-51d5-ae7d-a4b59234cedb" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5163 :tutorial/title "The Distance Between a Vector and a Subspace"} :step/id #uuid "7d1a7540-bb8b-5865-a0e0-852beed15e26" :step/math-academy-id 32460 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134821}} {:db/id 17592186134821 :step/content {:db/id 17592186133875 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186133691 :question/id #uuid "d7541321-4042-54af-9b64-59f255a6f1a3" :question/math-academy-id "e-8733"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "25e84fac-02c3-5111-98b3-bc67fe1ec9ab" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049274}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186134564} {:db/id 17592186134565} {:db/id 17592186241059} {:db/id 17592186241063} {:db/id 17592186241065} {:db/id 17592186241066} {:db/id 17592186241068} {:db/id 17592186241070} {:db/id 17592186241072} {:db/id 17592186241074} {:db/id 17592186375652} {:db/id 17592186543554}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Distance Between a Vector and a Subspace"} :step/id #uuid "20a627a4-468b-5c73-a4aa-e3ab9c87207e" :step/math-academy-id 32485 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134828}} {:db/id 17592186134828 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135107 :tutorial/content "The orthogonal projection of a vector $\mathbf{x}\in V$ onto $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}$ (or simply onto a vector $\mathbf{a}$) is the vector $\text{proj}_{\mathbf{a}}\,\mathbf{x}\in \textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}$ that is "closest" to $\mathbf{x}$ with respect to the distance defined by the inner product.

Although we've considered abstract vector spaces with any possible inner product in this lesson, we can still visualize this situation with the following diagram:

![](images/09/099a0bb20552824d2376994c3eb7145e48bbf78552d16de39fec44bda6b766f2.png)

As shown in the diagram, the projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}$ is the vector $\text{proj}_{\mathbf{a}}\,\mathbf{x}$ such that $\mathbf{x} - \text{proj}_{\mathbf{a}}\,\mathbf{x}$ is orthogonal to $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}.$

Furthermore, $\| \mathbf{x} - \text{proj}_{\mathbf{a}}\,\mathbf{x} \|$ will be the smallest possible distance (with respect to our inner product) from $\mathbf{x}$ to any vector in $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "629bc20f-76c3-5217-b763-e4ab0c831a8d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5343 :tutorial/title "The Intuition Behind Orthogonal Projections in Inner Product Spaces"} :step/id #uuid "97501e93-7a73-5f78-8d81-1f3d7a340746" :step/math-academy-id 33420} {:db/id 17592186134885 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135141 :tutorial/content "Consider the functions 

$$
f_1(t)=t,\qquad f_2(t)=t^2+1, \qquad h(t)= 5t^3,
$$

in the vector space $V = \mathcal{C}[-1,1]$ of continuous functions over $[-1,1],$ where the inner product is defined as

$$
\langle x(t),y(t) \rangle = \int_{-1}^1 x(t) y(t) \, \text{d}t.
$$

Let's find the orthogonal projection of $h(t)$ onto the subspace

$$
S= \textrm{Span}\{f_1(t), f_2(t)\},
$$

 

given that $f_1(t) \perp f_2(t)$ with respect to this inner product. 

Since the set $\{f_1(t),f_2(t)\}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $h(t)$ onto $S$ is given by

$$
\textrm{proj}_{S}\,h(t) 
= \textrm{proj}_{f_1(t)}\,h(t) + \textrm{proj}_{f_2(t)}\,h(t).
$$

Let's now compute these projections:

- First, we compute  the orthogonal projection of $h(t)$ onto $\textrm{Span}\{f_1(t)\}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,h(t) & =\frac{⟨h(t),{f}_{1}(t)⟩}{⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{1}(t)⟩}\,{f}_{1}(t) \\  & =\frac{{\int }_{-1}^{1}5{t}^{4}\,\text{d}t}{{\int }_{-1}^{1}{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t}\cdot t \\  & =3t\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we compute  the orthogonal projection of $h(t)$ onto $\textrm{Span}\{f_2(t)\}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,h(t) & =\frac{⟨h(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩}{⟨{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩}\,{f}_{2}(t) \\  & =\frac{{\int }_{-1}^{1}5{t}^{3}({t}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}t}{{\int }_{-1}^{1}({t}^{2}+1)^{2}\,\text{d}t}\cdot ({t}^{2}+1) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Note: We used the fact that the integrand in the numerator is an odd function, so its integral over $[-1,1]$ must be zero.

Finally, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,h(t) & ={\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,h(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,h(t) \\  & =3t+0 \\  & =3t.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "975c7894-a67f-5528-875e-2e55a94d99b9" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6130 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} :step/id #uuid "b89a94ac-0dd4-505c-b266-41783d527047" :step/math-academy-id 37245 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134818}}] :activity/title "Projecting Vectors Onto Subspaces in Inner Product Spaces" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186134005} {:db/id 17592186134817 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135105 :tutorial/content "Let $V$ be an inner product space with the inner product $\langle\cdot, \cdot\rangle.$ If

with respect to the inner product is given by

is a vector space equipped with an inner product $\left\langle\cdot, \cdot\right\rangle$ and that $\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{w} \in V.$ The **distance $d$ between $\mathbf v$ and $\mathbf w$ with respect to the inner product** is defined by the *norm* of $\mathbf{v}- \mathbf{w}.$ That is,

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =‖v-w‖=\sqrt{⟨v-w,v-w⟩}.\end{aligned}
$$

For example, suppose that $V = \mathcal{C}[0,1],$ the vector space of continuous functions over $[0,1],$ equipped with the inner product

$$
\langle x(t),y(t) \rangle = \int_0^{1} x(t) y(t) \, \text{d}t.
$$

The distance between the functions $f(t)=4t$ and $g(t)=t+1$ with respect to the given inner product is

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =‖f(t)-g(t)‖ \\  & =‖4t-(t+1)‖ \\  & =‖3t-1‖ \\  & =\sqrt{⟨3t-1,3t-1⟩} \\  & =\sqrt{{\int }_{0}^{1}(3t-1)^{2}\,\text{d}t} \\  & =\sqrt{{\frac{1}{9}\cdot (3t-1)^{3}|}_{0}^{1}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{9}\cdot [(8)-(-1)]} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{9}\cdot 9} \\  & =\sqrt{1} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

More generally, given an orthogonal set 

$$
\big\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 , \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n \big\} \subset  V
$$

and a vector $\mathbf x \in V,$  the **distance between $\mathbf{x}$ and the subspace** 

$$
S=\textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2,  \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n \}
$$

is defined as

$$
\Vert{ \color{black} \mathbf{x} - \text{proj}_{S}\,\mathbf{x} }\Vert.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "4ca26c36-a2e4-51d5-ae7d-a4b59234cedb" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5163 :tutorial/title "The Distance Between a Vector and a Subspace"} :step/id #uuid "7d1a7540-bb8b-5865-a0e0-852beed15e26" :step/math-academy-id 32460 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134821}} {:db/id 17592186135106 :tutorial/content "Suppose that $V$ is a vector space equipped with an inner product $\left\langle\cdot, \cdot\right\rangle$ and that $\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{w} \in V.$ The **distance $d$ between $\mathbf v$ and $\mathbf w$ with respect to the inner product** is defined by the *norm* of $\mathbf{v}- \mathbf{w}.$ That is,

As shown in the diagram, the projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}$ is the vector $\text{proj}_{\mathbf{a}}\,\mathbf{x}$ such that $\mathbf{x} - \text{proj}_{\mathbf{a}}\,\mathbf{x}$ is orthogonal to $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}.$

Furthermore, $\| \mathbf{x} - \text{proj}_{\mathbf{a}}\,\mathbf{x} \|$ will be the smallest possible distance (with respect to our inner product) from $\mathbf{x}$ to any vector in $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "629bc20f-76c3-5217-b763-e4ab0c831a8d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5343 :tutorial/title "The Intuition Behind Orthogonal Projections in Inner Product Spaces"} :step/id #uuid "97501e93-7a73-5f78-8d81-1f3d7a340746" :step/math-academy-id 33420} {:db/id 17592186135107 :tutorial/content "The orthogonal projection of a vector $\mathbf{x}\in V$ onto $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}$ (or simply onto a vector $\mathbf{a}$) is the vector $\text{proj}_{\mathbf{a}}\,\mathbf{x}\in \textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}$ that is "closest" to $\mathbf{x}$ with respect to the distance defined by the inner product.

Furthermore, $\| \mathbf{x} - \text{proj}_{\mathbf{a}}\,\mathbf{x} \|$ will be the smallest possible distance (with respect to our inner product) from $\mathbf{x}$ to any vector in $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "629bc20f-76c3-5217-b763-e4ab0c831a8d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5343 :tutorial/title "The Intuition Behind Orthogonal Projections in Inner Product Spaces"} {:db/id 17592186135141 :tutorial/content "Consider the functions 

$$
f_1(t)=t,\qquad f_2(t)=t^2+1, \qquad h(t)= 5t^3,
$$

in the vector space $V = \mathcal{C}[-1,1]$ of continuous functions over $[-1,1],$ where the inner product is defined as

$$
\langle x(t),y(t) \rangle = \int_{-1}^1 x(t) y(t) \, \text{d}t.
$$

Let's find the orthogonal projection of $h(t)$ onto the subspace

$$
S= \textrm{Span}\{f_1(t), f_2(t)\},
$$

 

given that $f_1(t) \perp f_2(t)$ with respect to this inner product. 

Since the set $\{f_1(t),f_2(t)\}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $h(t)$ onto $S$ is given by

$$
\textrm{proj}_{S}\,h(t) 
= \textrm{proj}_{f_1(t)}\,h(t) + \textrm{proj}_{f_2(t)}\,h(t).
$$

Let's now compute these projections:

- First, we compute  the orthogonal projection of $h(t)$ onto $\textrm{Span}\{f_1(t)\}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,h(t) & =\frac{⟨h(t),{f}_{1}(t)⟩}{⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{1}(t)⟩}\,{f}_{1}(t) \\  & =\frac{{\int }_{-1}^{1}5{t}^{4}\,\text{d}t}{{\int }_{-1}^{1}{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t}\cdot t \\  & =3t\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we compute  the orthogonal projection of $h(t)$ onto $\textrm{Span}\{f_2(t)\}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,h(t) & =\frac{⟨h(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩}{⟨{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩}\,{f}_{2}(t) \\  & =\frac{{\int }_{-1}^{1}5{t}^{3}({t}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}t}{{\int }_{-1}^{1}({t}^{2}+1)^{2}\,\text{d}t}\cdot ({t}^{2}+1) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Note: We used the fact that the integrand in the numerator is an odd function, so its integral over $[-1,1]$ must be zero.

Finally, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,h(t) & ={\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,h(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,h(t) \\  & =3t+0 \\  & =3t.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "975c7894-a67f-5528-875e-2e55a94d99b9" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6130 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} {:activity/course {:db/id 17592186046660} :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186413797} :activity/id #uuid "fba5b1da-9880-515c-af94-05681b35cd3b" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186050841 :topic/id #uuid "6aced1c3-bd0e-5b1d-973e-105b955f9e1a" :topic/math-academy-id 2126} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186413793 :step/content {:db/id 17592186134064 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "00a97740-bf4e-5245-a223-1105ad76868c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\operatorname{cos}⁡t" :db/id 17592186238086} {:answer/id #uuid "0ccb496a-1f3e-5f9c-9be5-7756bb97a385" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186238169} {:answer/id #uuid "9dbfd16e-b04d-5762-91cf-d69f6af7923d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186239432} {:answer/id #uuid "a5578604-9539-5565-8bbb-579ff2d23c8a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186239490} {:answer/id #uuid "ff74f82e-113d-5ba7-9d63-962e019ecfd4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186240320}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186238086} :answer-field/id #uuid "50e2f23b-8197-5ffd-805f-f3ecff761a73" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186240475}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "e7a8c44b-b300-5e66-9428-e03f400ebf5f" :question/math-academy-id "q-105416" :question/problem "Let $V=C[-\pi ,\pi ],$ the vector space of continuous functions over $[-\pi ,\pi ]$, and let the inner product on $V$ be defined as

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Now consider the following elements of $V:$

$$
{f}_{1}(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,{f}_{2}(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,g(t)={sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $S=\text{Span}\{{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)\}$ given that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the inner product, and that the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $\text{Span}\{{f}_{2}(t)\}$ equals $-\operatorname{cos}⁡t.$" :question/worked-solution "Since the set $\{{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)\}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,g(t)={\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t).
$$

We are given that ${\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t)=-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,$ so let's now find the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $\text{Span}\{{f}_{1}(t)\}.$ This can be computed as

$$
{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)=\frac{⟨g(t),{f}_{1}(t)⟩}{⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{1}(t)⟩}\,{f}_{1}(t).
$$

 

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨g(t),{f}_{1}(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(t){f}_{1}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }({sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t({sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ is an odd function, while ${sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ is even. Hence, their product $\operatorname{sin}⁡t({sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)$ must be an odd function. Now, since we have an integral over the interval $[-\pi ,\pi ],$ which is symmetric about the origin, we can conclude that

$$
{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t({sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,\text{d}t=0.
$$

  

Therefore,

$$
{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)=\frac{0}{⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{1}(t)⟩}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t=0.
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,g(t) & ={\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t) \\  & =0-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "0a412cdd-29f8-5273-ab55-2a8dce391dae" :step/next {:db/id 17592186413795}} {:db/id 17592186413794 :step/content {:db/id 17592186241003 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1a9db971-884b-5cf9-9a84-c91c9fa4fa01" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8+\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186238276} {:answer/id #uuid "39658250-b0fe-59bb-a334-a4e517b0d75e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2-\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186238550} {:answer/id #uuid "880b7d31-ec04-56db-ad2a-f754621f1b8d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1-\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186239237} {:answer/id #uuid "b1b15087-e383-5255-8efc-84ad43c168b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186239607} {:answer/id #uuid "cd180c30-2f84-5a24-af62-8965f36db06d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186239851}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186239607} :answer-field/id #uuid "51c982ce-3e72-5b74-bcb0-6eb543685681" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186240480}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "2bf55fb2-ca86-5707-a52a-d891899878f4" :question/math-academy-id "q-105186" :question/problem "Let $V=C[-\pi ,\pi ],$ the vector space of continuous functions over $[-\pi ,\pi ]$, and let the inner product on $V$ be defined as

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Now consider the following elements of $V:$

$$
{f}_{1}(t)=2,\,{f}_{2}(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,g(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t+6
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $S=\text{Span}\{{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)\}$ given that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the inner product, and that the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $\text{Span}\{{f}_{1}(t)\}$ equals $6.$" :question/worked-solution "Since the set $\{{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)\}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,g(t)={\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t).
$$

We are given that ${\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)=6,$ so let's now find the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $\text{Span}\{{f}_{2}(t)\}.$ This can be computed as

$$
{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t)=\frac{⟨g(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩}{⟨{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩}\,{f}_{2}(t).
$$

 

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨g(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(t){f}_{2}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t+6)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t-2{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t+6{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ is an odd function, while $\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ is even. Hence, their product $\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ must be an odd function. Now, since we have integrals over the interval $[-\pi ,\pi ],$ which is symmetric about the origin, we can conclude that

$$
{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t=0.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨g(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩ & =-2{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t) & =\frac{-2{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t}{⟨{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =\frac{-2{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t}{{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,g(t) & ={\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t) \\  & =6-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "0bc7e18b-fdb5-5429-828f-e671a9abcbda" :step/next {:db/id 17592186413793}} {:db/id 17592186413795 :step/content {:db/id 17592186241059 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "694bbe7e-1033-5685-8db7-c579e340a4af" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186238969} {:answer/id #uuid "7187a2ab-aec2-5516-9817-82c6b1e6f0ad" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186239028} {:answer/id #uuid "98f9f087-a4cb-5b2b-ba88-6c34977c1ab6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{5}" :db/id 17592186239383} {:answer/id #uuid "d0b7eedf-e87f-53c1-a7c0-62ebe727a2fa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186239882} {:answer/id #uuid "f69f76e8-1b93-5cd1-b517-2cdfc888efb3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186240229}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186239028} :answer-field/id #uuid "eabf99e8-310f-5528-b7c0-2d81c99774f8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186240742}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "a70f1b99-0d4b-5ef2-9e7e-0dc7f6d78417" :question/math-academy-id "q-105461" :question/problem "Let $V=C[0,1],$ the vector space of functions that are continuous over $[0,1].$ Given that the inner product on $V$ is defined as 

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{1}x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t,
$$

find the distance between $f(t)=3t$ and $g(t)=-3t+3$ with respect to the inner product." :question/worked-solution "The distance between $f(t)=3t$ and $g(t)=-3t+3$ with respect to the given inner product is

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =‖f(t)-g(t)‖ \\  & =‖3t-(-3t+3)‖ \\  & =‖6t-3‖ \\  & =\sqrt{⟨6t-3,6t-3⟩}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

We are given that ${\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t,$ so let's now find the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $\text{Span}\{{f}_{2}(t)\}.$ This can be computed as

$$
{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t)=\frac{⟨g(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩}{⟨{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩}\,{f}_{2}(t).

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨g(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(t){f}_{2}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t+1)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =5{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t-4{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ is an odd function, while $\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ is even. Hence, their product $\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ must be an odd function. Now, since we have an integral over the interval $[-\pi ,\pi ],$ which is symmetric about the origin, we can conclude that

$$
{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t=0.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨g(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩ & =-4{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Now consider the following elements of $V:$

$$
{f}_{1}(t)=2,\,{f}_{2}(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,g(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t+6
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $S=\text{Span}\{{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)\}$ given that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the inner product, and that the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $\text{Span}\{{f}_{1}(t)\}$ equals $6.$" :question/worked-solution "Since the set $\{{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)\}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,g(t)={\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t).
$$

We are given that ${\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)=6,$ so let's now find the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $\text{Span}\{{f}_{2}(t)\}.$ This can be computed as

$$
{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t)=\frac{⟨g(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩}{⟨{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩}\,{f}_{2}(t).
$$

 

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨g(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(t){f}_{2}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t+6)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t-2{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t+6{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ is an odd function, while $\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ is even. Hence, their product $\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ must be an odd function. Now, since we have integrals over the interval $[-\pi ,\pi ],$ which is symmetric about the origin, we can conclude that

$$
{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t=0.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨g(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩ & =-2{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t) & =\frac{-2{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t}{⟨{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =\frac{-2{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t}{{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,g(t) & ={\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t) \\  & =6-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "0bc7e18b-fdb5-5429-828f-e671a9abcbda" :step/next {:db/id 17592186413793}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1a9db971-884b-5cf9-9a84-c91c9fa4fa01" :answer/type {:db/id Given that the inner product on $V$ is defined as 

$$
⟨p(t),q(t)⟩=p(0)q(0)+p(1)q(1),
$$

find the distance between $f(t)=4t$ and $g(t)=3t-3$ with respect to the inner product." :question/worked-solution "The distance between $f(t)=4t$ and $g(t)=3t-3$ with respect to the given inner product is

$$

$$

Computing the inner product, we get

$$

We are given that ${\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t)=-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,$ so let's now find the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $\text{Span}\{{f}_{1}(t)\}.$ This can be computed as
